1	Review
2	
3	                                                                            Perceptual and Motor Skills
4	                                                                            2023, Vol. 0(0) 1–27
5	Relationship Between                                                        © The Author(s) 2023
6	                                                                            Article reuse guidelines:
7	Athletes’ History of Stressors                                              sagepub.com/journals-permissions
8	                                                                            DOI: 10.1177/00315125231216329
9	                                                                            journals.sagepub.com/home/pms
10	and Sport Injury: A Systematic
11	Review and Meta-Analysis
12	
13	
14	Theresa Chyi1, Frank J. H. Lu1 , Yun-Che Hsieh1,2 ,
15	Ya-Wen Hsu3, Diane L. Gill4, and Bin-Bin Fang5
16	
17	
18	Abstract
19	A history of stressors in athletes represents psychosocial factors that may lead to sport
20	injury. However, empirical studies have provided varying results for the relationship
21	between stress history and sport injury. We examined prior literature on the stress
22	history - sport injury relationship within a systematic review and, by meta-analysis, we
23	offered a pooled estimate of the strength of this relationship. We searched seven major
24	academic databases (Sportdiscus, Psyinfo, Academic Search Premier, Ovid, Scopus,
25	Web of Science, and PubMed) from January 2000 to September 2023 and identiﬁed
26	19 empirical studies that examined injuries in sports contexts for meta-analysis. In
27	19 empirical studies of moderate to high publication quality, we found moderate
28	heterogeneity (Q(17) = 98.61; p < .001), low sensitivity (I2 77.82–83.77), and low
29	publication bias (Z-value = 7.74; p < .001). Further, using a random effect estimate-r,
30	we found a low but signiﬁcant correlation between stress history and sport injury,
31	yielding a small overall effect size (ES) of r = .12. Furthermore, moderation analyses
32	found adolescents (r = .14), contact-sport athletes (r = .09), non-elite athletes (r = .13),
33	and non-European athletes (America r = .16; Asia r = .14; Oceania r = .14) to have a
34	
35	
36	1
37	  Graduate Institute of Sport Coaching Science, Chinese Culture University, Taipei, Taiwan
38	2
39	  Department of Sport Sciences, Army Academy, R.O.C., Taipei, Taiwan
40	3
41	  Department of Physical Education, Health, and Recreation, National Chiayi University, Chiayi, Taiwan
42	4
43	  Department of Kinesiology, University of North Carolina at Greensboro, Greensboro, NC, USA
44	5
45	  School of Physical Education, Quanzhou Normal University, Quanzhou, China
46	
47	Corresponding Author:
48	Frank J. H. Lu, Graduate Institute of Sport Coaching Science, Chinese Culture University, 55, Hua-Kang Road,
49	Yang-Ming-Shan, Taipei 11114, Taiwan.
50	Email: frankjlu@gmail.com
51	 2                                                         Perceptual and Motor Skills 0(0)
52	
53	relatively higher ES than their counterparts in this stress history/sport injury
54	relationship. We concluded that inevitable life stressors may lead to many negative
55	consequences for athletes, such that sports professionals should provide stress
56	management educational programs to enhance athletes’ health and well-being.
57	
58	
59	Keywords
60	stress-illness, stress-accident, life stress, athletic trauma, psychology of sport injury,
61	health psychology
62	
63	
64	
65	Introduction
66	Sport injury is a prevailing phenomenon in the athletic world, with an estimated of
67	10,000 hours of sports training and competition resulting in 636 injury cases in rugby,
68	422 in soccer, 402 in hockey, 193 in badminton, 100 in tennis, and 179 in running
69	(Bueno et al., 2018). A Danish investigation of 10,000 adults found that 18.4% of adults
70	experienced sport injury; males had higher injury rates than females, and running,
71	soccer, and weight training had a higher incidence of sport injury than other sports.
72	Similarly, Luiggi and Griffet (2019) investigated 1360 French sports participants and
73	found that high-level athletes had a higher odds ratio for sport injury than low-to-
74	medium-level athletes. Speciﬁcally, basketball players had a higher odds ratio in sports
75	injury than handball, boxing, soccer, and gymnastics. In the 2017 Pyeongchang Winter
76	Olympic Games, Soligard et al. (2019) cooperated with the International Olympic
77	Committee (IOC) and 92 National Olympic Committees (NOCs) to investigate
78	2914 Olympic athletes’ injury experiences. During 17 days of the Olympiad, they
79	found 376 athletes (12.6%) reported sport injury, with the highest sport injury rates in
80	ski halfpipe (28%), snowboard cross (26%), ski cross (25%), snowboard slopestyle
81	(21%), and aerials (20%).
82	   Once a sport injury occurs, injured athletes must engage in a rehabilitation program
83	that includes injury assessments, treatments, and rehabilitation offered by medical staff
84	(Santi & Pietrantoni, 2013). Athletes may then experience temporary restrictions from
85	sports participation and psychological disturbance during rehabilitation. Speciﬁcally,
86	Wiese-Bjornstal et al. (1998) contended that pre-injury and post-injury factors inter-
87	actively inﬂuence injured athletes’ psychological responses in a dynamic and bi-
88	directional fashion. Further, personal and situational factors interact to inﬂuence injured
89	athletes’ cognitive (e.g., self-efﬁcacy, career goals, perceived competence), emotional
90	(e.g., anger, fear, depression), and behavioral (e.g., adhering to rehabilitation, substance
91	abuse, or taking risky behavior) responses. Through the process of rehabilitation,
92	injured athletes may eventually reach psychological and physical recovery, after which
93	further sport injury may inﬂuence not only the athletes’ physical conditions but also
94	their psychological well-being. In some extreme cases, injured athletes experience
95	major depression (Appaneal et al., 2009), anxiety (Rice et al., 2019), suicidal intention
96	 Chyi et al.                                                                                 3
97	
98	(Smith & Milliner, 1994), substance abuse (de Grace et al., 2017), and career ter-
99	mination (Ristolainen et al., 2012).
100	    Because sport injury is so prevalent and inﬂuences injured athletes’ physical and
101	mental health, many researchers have investigated the antecedents/causes of sport
102	injury. Generally, researchers have proposed that both internal factors (e.g., over-
103	training, physical ﬁtness, skill level, and psychological factors) and external factors
104	(e.g., nature of sports, types of equipment, facilities, and ﬁeld conditions) contribute to
105	sport injury (Bahr & Krosshaug, 2005). Some researchers speciﬁcally suggested that
106	psychological stress is a signiﬁcant cause of sport injury (Petrie, 1993). In highly
107	competitive settings, such as the Olympic Games, World Championships, and pro-
108	fessional tournaments, competitors experience multiple stressors, including training
109	adjustment, logistic adaptation, social expectations, media relations, interpersonal
110	competitions/conﬂicts, and organizational demands (Fletcher & Arnold, 2016). Ath-
111	letic stress, an inevitable part of competitive sports, can lead to injuries as well as
112	negative consequences such as burnout (Lin et al., 2022), physical illness (Humphrey
113	et al., 2000), depression (Nixdorf et al., 2020), and decreased performance (Nippert &
114	Smith, 2008). Thus, it is imperative to examine how stress may inﬂuence sport injury.
115	    Based on an integration of the stress-illness, stress-accident, and stress-injuries
116	literature, Williams and Andersen (1998) proposed that, in stressful athletic situations,
117	psychosocial factors such as personality (e.g., trait anxiety, hardiness), history of
118	stressors (e.g. negative life-events, past injury, and daily hassle), and coping (e.g., stress
119	management, social support) solely or jointly inﬂuence athletes’ cognitive appraisal of
120	the balance between environmental demands and coping resources. Once perceived
121	demands outweigh resources and outcomes, stress responses are triggered, such as
122	heightened muscle tension, increased blood pressure, and elevated heart rate. Stress
123	may also change cognitive functions, precipitating negative thoughts and narrowing
124	attention to cause further sports injuries.
125	    Following Williams and Andersen’s (1998) stress-sport injury model, many re-
126	searchers examined psychosocial factors contributing to sport injury. Among four
127	major categories of psychosocial factors (i.e., personality, history of stressors, coping
128	resources, and intervention), athletes’ history of stressors has received the most re-
129	search attention. A history of stressors includes major life events, daily hassles, and
130	history of previous injury. According to stimulus-based theories of stress (Cooper,
131	2015), disturbing life events such as the death of a loved one, divorce, getting ﬁred, and
132	bad relationships strongly impact health and illness (Slavich, 2016). Because stress is
133	embedded in competitive sports and has been found to be associated with athletes’
134	health-related problems (Nimmo & Ekblom, 2007), it is important to understand the
135	inﬂuence of the history of stressors on sport injury.
136	    In a study examining the relationship between social stressors (coaches, teammates)
137	and acute/chronic injury, Pensgaard et al. (2017) sampled 193 elite Norwegian female
138	handball/football players. They measured life stress and perceived motivational climate
139	at the beginning of the season and then recorded injury records through the rest of the
140	season. Perceived negative life event stress from teammates was associated with an
141	 4                                                         Perceptual and Motor Skills 0(0)
142	
143	increased risk of acute injuries (OR = 1.23), and there was a signiﬁcant relationship
144	between the coach’s perceived negative life event stress and risk of overuse injuries
145	(OR = 1.21).
146	    Li et al. (2019), in a prospective research design, examined relationships among
147	112 college student athletes’ basic psychological needs, satisfaction/frustration, stress
148	responses, and sports injury. They measured participants’ basic psychological need
149	satisfaction/frustration and perceived stress during the study’s ﬁrst three months and
150	then used self-report injury records in the second, third, and fourth months. They found
151	that basic psychological need satisfaction had direct negative effects on sports injuries
152	(R2 = 18), and stress directly affected sport injury (R2 = .29). Further, they found that
153	basic psychological need satisfaction had an indirect effect on injury occurrence via
154	stress.
155	    Although these studies provide initial data on the relationship between stress history
156	and sport injury, a pooled estimate across studies to summarize research ﬁndings on this
157	relationship has yet to be produced. In past research, several investigators used general
158	life stress scales (e.g., Perceived Stress Scale; PSS; Cohen et al., 1983; The Hassle and
159	Uplift Scale, HUS; DeLongis et al., 1988), while others used sport-speciﬁc measures
160	such as The Athletic Life Experiences Survey (ALES; Passer & Seese, 1983) and The
161	Life Events Survey for Collegiate Athletes (LESCA; Petrie, 1992). Whether inves-
162	tigators revealed different ﬁndings with different measures remains unknown. Further,
163	some research sampled youth athletes while others recruited senior athletes, and
164	whether age moderates the relationship needs further examination (Rogers & Werthner,
165	2022). Sport type is also a relevant variable, as contact sports (e.g., basketball, boxing,
166	rugby) versus non-contact sports (e.g., golf, tennis, archery) might moderate the history
167	of stressors-sport injury relationship.
168	    Based on this background literature, we examined past research addressing the
169	relationship between the history of stressors and sport injury in a systematic review and
170	by meta-analysis. We hoped to gain a pooled estimate of the strength of the relationship
171	between history of stressors and sport injury. In addition, we attempted to examine
172	whether this relationship was moderated by athletes’ age, athletes’ competition level,
173	sport type, region, and stress measurement scale.
174	
175	
176	Method
177	Article Search Strategy
178	We adopted the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis
179	(PRISMA, Page et al., 2021) statement to guide our study. First, we designed a
180	comprehensive search strategy to select eligible studies that examined the history of
181	stressors-sport injury relationships. We searched seven academic databases: Sport-
182	discus, Psyinfo, Scopus, Web of Science, Academic Search Premier, Ovid, and
183	PubMed from January 2000 to September 2023. We used the following keywords to
184	identify relevant articles (adding a Boolean operator [OR and/or AND] to combine
185	 Chyi et al.                                                                                 5
186	
187	them: (a) stress OR distress OR pressure OR hassle, (b) injury, (c) psychological
188	predictor*, and (d) athlete* OR sport* OR player*. Finally, we included only peer-
189	reviewed publications available in English.
190	
191	Eligibility Criteria. In the ﬁrst phase of this review, the ﬁrst and second authors of this
192	paper (TC and FJL) conducted separate searches using the same methodology. Ad-
193	ditionally, they each used reference lists from selected papers to search for additional
194	articles on Google Scholar. Following this phase, these two authors independently
195	evaluated each article’s title, abstract, and full text to determine their relevance to this
196	review. They double-checked each other’s individual search results to ensure that
197	relevant articles had been selected. If there was a difference in whether an article was
198	judged to be relevant, the third author (YCH) made the ﬁnal decision.
199	    Initially, this search produced 256 articles from online databases. After removing
200	124 duplicate articles, there were 132 articles from online databases and eight addi-
201	tional articles from other sources. We also screened the titles and abstracts of these
202	remaining articles to determine those that might be subjected to meta-analysis. We
203	excluded articles on the basis of the following criteria: (a) the sample was unrelated to
204	injury or stress in athletes, and (b) the article did not involve quantitative analysis. After
205	these procedures, we obtained and evaluated the full texts of just 15 online articles. In
206	the full-text screening, we excluded articles based on the following further criteria: (a)
207	injury/stress data were not obtained; (b) data were incomplete (e.g., lacking mean,
208	standard deviation, r-value, R2, p-value); and (c) athlete stress was not compared/
209	associated with injury. Ten studies were excluded because they failed to meet the
210	selection criteria, leaving ﬁve online articles. In addition, we searched the eight articles
211	that had been drawn from reference lists in other articles, and using the same procedures
212	to ﬁlter them, we excluded ﬁve studies. Thus, eleven articles from the previous review
213	by Ivarsson et al. (2017) and eight articles from the searching, selecting, and screening
214	process in the present study were collected (ﬁve studies via databases and three studies
215	via other methods) so that we included a total of 19 studies for analysis (Figure 1).
216	
217	Article Quality Assessment. After initial selection based on the criteria above, we adopted
218	Glasziou et al.’s (2001) suggestion to evaluate the quality of the included studies. To
219	evaluate all included studies, Kmet et al. (2004) proposed “14 evaluation questions” for
220	the quality assessment of quantitative studies (Table 1). Two co-authors with expertise
221	in sports psychology research (BBF and FJL) independently coded article quality
222	according to Kmet et al.’s proposed scheme, and we only included studies with higher
223	than moderate scores (i.e., those meeting at least 60% of the criteria).
224	
225	Meta-Analytic Strategies. We used Comprehensive Meta-Analysis (CMA) statistical
226	software 4.0 to analyze the stress history/sport injury relationships with the 19 included
227	studies. The CMA allows researchers to combine observational and experimental
228	studies. So, we used correlation coefﬁcients, means and standard deviations, t test
229	values, Fisher’s z, p-values, sample sizes, and odds ratios (OR) as data inputs for this
230	 6                                                         Perceptual and Motor Skills 0(0)
231	
232	
233	
234	
235	Figure 1. PRISMA Flow Chart of the Studies Included in the Systematic Review and Meta-
236	Analysis.
237	
238	
239	meta-analysis. We applied a random-effects model to conceptualize the meta-analysis
240	and generate ﬁnal study ﬁndings (i.e., unconditional inferences). Further, if a single
241	article reported multiple results, all results within that single article were combined into
242	one metric so that the meta-analysis was balanced across all studies.
243	    We performed a sensitivity analysis of our articles by using the leave-one-out
244	method (i.e., deleting one study at a time and repeating the analysis) to assess the
245	stability of the meta-analysis. We used a Q-test to examine whether the true effect size
246	(ES) varied between studies when a random effect was applied (i.e., heterogeneity,
247	Tufanaru et al., 2015). A signiﬁcant Q-value reﬂected heterogeneity between samples.
248	In addition, the I2 statistic indicated different levels of heterogeneity at 25% (low
249	degree), 50% (moderate degree), and 75% (high degree) (Higgins et al., 2003). We used
250	I2 to interpret the magnitude of heterogeneity for signiﬁcant Q-values.
251	    Publication bias is common in meta-analysis because unpublished articles, often
252	with null effects, are excluded from such analysis. We evaluated publication bias with
253	the Fail-safe number (N, Nf.s) test (Field & Gillett, 2010) and Funnel Plot (Verhagen &
254	Ferreira, 2014). A relatively high fail-safe number indicates publication bias. We used a
255	forest plot to represent the ES and 95% conﬁdence intervals (CIs) to indicate the
256	correlation between the two variables (Marks-Anglin et al., 2021). We adopted
257	McGrath and Meyer’s suggestion that values of .37, .24, and .10 represent large,
258	medium, and small ES. The ES was considered statistically signiﬁcant at the p <
259	.05 level if the CI did not include zero.

297	Descriptions of Study Characteristics
298	The included 19 studies were published between January 2000 and September 2023.
299	These articles were conducted in four different continents: eleven in Europe (Sweden =

306	classiﬁed as contact sports, three as non-contact sports, and two as mixed. Seven studies

Review and Meta-Analysis


Theresa Chyi1, Frank J. H. Lu1 , Yun-Che Hsieh1,2 ,
Ya-Wen Hsu3, Diane L. Gill4, and Bin-Bin Fang5


Abstract
A history of stressors in athletes represents psychosocial factors that may lead to sport
injury. However, empirical studies have provided varying results for the relationship
between stress history and sport injury. We examined prior literature on the stress
history - sport injury relationship within a systematic review and, by meta-analysis, we
offered a pooled estimate of the strength of this relationship. We searched seven major
academic databases (Sportdiscus, Psyinfo, Academic Search Premier, Ovid, Scopus,
Web of Science, and PubMed) from January 2000 to September 2023 and identiﬁed
19 empirical studies that examined injuries in sports contexts for meta-analysis. In
19 empirical studies of moderate to high publication quality, we found moderate
heterogeneity (Q(17) = 98.61; p < .001), low sensitivity (I2 77.82–83.77), and low
publication bias (Z-value = 7.74; p < .001). Further, using a random effect estimate-r,
we found a low but signiﬁcant correlation between stress history and sport injury,
yielding a small overall effect size (ES) of r = .12. Furthermore, moderation analyses
found adolescents (r = .14), contact-sport athletes (r = .09), non-elite athletes (r = .13),
and non-European athletes (America r = .16; Asia r = .14; Oceania r = .14) to have a

Keywords
stress-illness, stress-accident, life stress, athletic trauma, psychology of sport injury,
health psychology



Introduction
Sport injury is a prevailing phenomenon in the athletic world, with an estimated of
10,000 hours of sports training and competition resulting in 636 injury cases in rugby,
422 in soccer, 402 in hockey, 193 in badminton, 100 in tennis, and 179 in running
(Bueno et al., 2018). A Danish investigation of 10,000 adults found that 18.4% of adults
experienced sport injury; males had higher injury rates than females, and running,
soccer, and weight training had a higher incidence of sport injury than other sports.
Similarly, Luiggi and Griffet (2019) investigated 1360 French sports participants and
found that high-level athletes had a higher odds ratio for sport injury than low-to-
medium-level athletes. Speciﬁcally, basketball players had a higher odds ratio in sports
injury than handball, boxing, soccer, and gymnastics. In the 2017 Pyeongchang Winter
Olympic Games, Soligard et al. (2019) cooperated with the International Olympic
Committee (IOC) and 92 National Olympic Committees (NOCs) to investigate
2914 Olympic athletes’ injury experiences. During 17 days of the Olympiad, they
found 376 athletes (12.6%) reported sport injury, with the highest sport injury rates in
ski halfpipe (28%), snowboard cross (26%), ski cross (25%), snowboard slopestyle
(21%), and aerials (20%).
   Once a sport injury occurs, injured athletes must engage in a rehabilitation program
that includes injury assessments, treatments, and rehabilitation offered by medical staff
(Santi & Pietrantoni, 2013). Athletes may then experience temporary restrictions from
sports participation and psychological disturbance during rehabilitation. Speciﬁcally,
Wiese-Bjornstal et al. (1998) contended that pre-injury and post-injury factors inter-
actively inﬂuence injured athletes’ psychological responses in a dynamic and bi-
directional fashion. Further, personal and situational factors interact to inﬂuence injured
athletes’ cognitive (e.g., self-efﬁcacy, career goals, perceived competence), emotional
(e.g., anger, fear, depression), and behavioral (e.g., adhering to rehabilitation, substance
abuse, or taking risky behavior) responses. Through the process of rehabilitation,
injured athletes may eventually reach psychological and physical recovery, after which
further sport injury may inﬂuence not only the athletes’ physical conditions but also
their psychological well-being. In some extreme cases, injured athletes experience
major depression (Appaneal et al., 2009), anxiety (Rice et al., 2019), suicidal intention
 Chyi et al.                                                                                 3

(Smith & Milliner, 1994), substance abuse (de Grace et al., 2017), and career ter-
mination (Ristolainen et al., 2012).
    Because sport injury is so prevalent and inﬂuences injured athletes’ physical and
mental health, many researchers have investigated the antecedents/causes of sport
injury. Generally, researchers have proposed that both internal factors (e.g., over-
training, physical ﬁtness, skill level, and psychological factors) and external factors
(e.g., nature of sports, types of equipment, facilities, and ﬁeld conditions) contribute to
sport injury (Bahr & Krosshaug, 2005). Some researchers speciﬁcally suggested that
psychological stress is a signiﬁcant cause of sport injury (Petrie, 1993). In highly
competitive settings, such as the Olympic Games, World Championships, and pro-
fessional tournaments, competitors experience multiple stressors, including training
adjustment, logistic adaptation, social expectations, media relations, interpersonal
competitions/conﬂicts, and organizational demands (Fletcher & Arnold, 2016). Ath-
letic stress, an inevitable part of competitive sports, can lead to injuries as well as
negative consequences such as burnout (Lin et al., 2022), physical illness (Humphrey
et al., 2000), depression (Nixdorf et al., 2020), and decreased performance (Nippert &
Smith, 2008). Thus, it is imperative to examine how stress may inﬂuence sport injury.
    Based on an integration of the stress-illness, stress-accident, and stress-injuries
literature, Williams and Andersen (1998) proposed that, in stressful athletic situations,
psychosocial factors such as personality (e.g., trait anxiety, hardiness), history of
stressors (e.g. negative life-events, past injury, and daily hassle), and coping (e.g., stress
management, social support) solely or jointly inﬂuence athletes’ cognitive appraisal of
the balance between environmental demands and coping resources. Once perceived
demands outweigh resources and outcomes, stress responses are triggered, such as
heightened muscle tension, increased blood pressure, and elevated heart rate. Stress
may also change cognitive functions, precipitating negative thoughts and narrowing
attention to cause further sports injuries.
    Following Williams and Andersen’s (1998) stress-sport injury model, many re-
searchers examined psychosocial factors contributing to sport injury. Among four
major categories of psychosocial factors (i.e., personality, history of stressors, coping
resources, and intervention), athletes’ history of stressors has received the most re-
search attention. A history of stressors includes major life events, daily hassles, and
history of previous injury. According to stimulus-based theories of stress (Cooper,
2015), disturbing life events such as the death of a loved one, divorce, getting ﬁred, and
bad relationships strongly impact health and illness (Slavich, 2016). Because stress is
embedded in competitive sports and has been found to be associated with athletes’
health-related problems (Nimmo & Ekblom, 2007), it is important to understand the
inﬂuence of the history of stressors on sport injury.
    In a study examining the relationship between social stressors (coaches, teammates)
and acute/chronic injury, Pensgaard et al. (2017) sampled 193 elite Norwegian female
handball/football players. They measured life stress and perceived motivational climate
at the beginning of the season and then recorded injury records through the rest of the
season. Perceived negative life event stress from teammates was associated with an
 4                                                         Perceptual and Motor Skills 0(0)

increased risk of acute injuries (OR = 1.23), and there was a signiﬁcant relationship
between the coach’s perceived negative life event stress and risk of overuse injuries
(OR = 1.21).
    Li et al. (2019), in a prospective research design, examined relationships among
112 college student athletes’ basic psychological needs, satisfaction/frustration, stress
responses, and sports injury. They measured participants’ basic psychological need
satisfaction/frustration and perceived stress during the study’s ﬁrst three months and
then used self-report injury records in the second, third, and fourth months. They found
that basic psychological need satisfaction had direct negative effects on sports injuries
(R2 = 18), and stress directly affected sport injury (R2 = .29). Further, they found that
basic psychological need satisfaction had an indirect effect on injury occurrence via
stress.
    Although these studies provide initial data on the relationship between stress history
and sport injury, a pooled estimate across studies to summarize research ﬁndings on this
relationship has yet to be produced. In past research, several investigators used general
life stress scales (e.g., Perceived Stress Scale; PSS; Cohen et al., 1983; The Hassle and
Uplift Scale, HUS; DeLongis et al., 1988), while others used sport-speciﬁc measures
such as The Athletic Life Experiences Survey (ALES; Passer & Seese, 1983) and The
Life Events Survey for Collegiate Athletes (LESCA; Petrie, 1992). Whether inves-
tigators revealed different ﬁndings with different measures remains unknown. Further,
some research sampled youth athletes while others recruited senior athletes, and
whether age moderates the relationship needs further examination (Rogers & Werthner,
2022). Sport type is also a relevant variable, as contact sports (e.g., basketball, boxing,
rugby) versus non-contact sports (e.g., golf, tennis, archery) might moderate the history
of stressors-sport injury relationship.
    Based on this background literature, we examined past research addressing the
relationship between the history of stressors and sport injury in a systematic review and
by meta-analysis. We hoped to gain a pooled estimate of the strength of the relationship
between history of stressors and sport injury. In addition, we attempted to examine
whether this relationship was moderated by athletes’ age, athletes’ competition level,
sport type, region, and stress measurement scale.


Method
Article Search Strategy
We adopted the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis
(PRISMA, Page et al., 2021) statement to guide our study. First, we designed a
comprehensive search strategy to select eligible studies that examined the history of
stressors-sport injury relationships. We searched seven academic databases: Sport-
discus, Psyinfo, Scopus, Web of Science, Academic Search Premier, Ovid, and
PubMed from January 2000 to September 2023. We used the following keywords to
identify relevant articles (adding a Boolean operator [OR and/or AND] to combine
 Chyi et al.                                                                                 5

them: (a) stress OR distress OR pressure OR hassle, (b) injury, (c) psychological
predictor*, and (d) athlete* OR sport* OR player*. Finally, we included only peer-
reviewed publications available in English.

Eligibility Criteria. In the ﬁrst phase of this review, the ﬁrst and second authors of this
paper (TC and FJL) conducted separate searches using the same methodology. Ad-
ditionally, they each used reference lists from selected papers to search for additional
articles on Google Scholar. Following this phase, these two authors independently
evaluated each article’s title, abstract, and full text to determine their relevance to this
review. They double-checked each other’s individual search results to ensure that
relevant articles had been selected. If there was a difference in whether an article was
judged to be relevant, the third author (YCH) made the ﬁnal decision.
    Initially, this search produced 256 articles from online databases. After removing
124 duplicate articles, there were 132 articles from online databases and eight addi-
tional articles from other sources. We also screened the titles and abstracts of these
remaining articles to determine those that might be subjected to meta-analysis. We
excluded articles on the basis of the following criteria: (a) the sample was unrelated to
injury or stress in athletes, and (b) the article did not involve quantitative analysis. After
these procedures, we obtained and evaluated the full texts of just 15 online articles. In
the full-text screening, we excluded articles based on the following further criteria: (a)
injury/stress data were not obtained; (b) data were incomplete (e.g., lacking mean,
standard deviation, r-value, R2, p-value); and (c) athlete stress was not compared/
associated with injury. Ten studies were excluded because they failed to meet the
selection criteria, leaving ﬁve online articles. In addition, we searched the eight articles
that had been drawn from reference lists in other articles, and using the same procedures
to ﬁlter them, we excluded ﬁve studies. Thus, eleven articles from the previous review
by Ivarsson et al. (2017) and eight articles from the searching, selecting, and screening
process in the present study were collected (ﬁve studies via databases and three studies
via other methods) so that we included a total of 19 studies for analysis (Figure 1).

Article Quality Assessment. After initial selection based on the criteria above, we adopted
Glasziou et al.’s (2001) suggestion to evaluate the quality of the included studies. To
evaluate all included studies, Kmet et al. (2004) proposed “14 evaluation questions” for
the quality assessment of quantitative studies (Table 1). Two co-authors with expertise
in sports psychology research (BBF and FJL) independently coded article quality
according to Kmet et al.’s proposed scheme, and we only included studies with higher
than moderate scores (i.e., those meeting at least 60% of the criteria).

Meta-Analytic Strategies. We used Comprehensive Meta-Analysis (CMA) statistical
software 4.0 to analyze the stress history/sport injury relationships with the 19 included
studies. The CMA allows researchers to combine observational and experimental
studies. So, we used correlation coefﬁcients, means and standard deviations, t test
values, Fisher’s z, p-values, sample sizes, and odds ratios (OR) as data inputs for this
 6                                                         Perceptual and Motor Skills 0(0)

meta-analysis. We applied a random-effects model to conceptualize the meta-analysis
and generate ﬁnal study ﬁndings (i.e., unconditional inferences). Further, if a single
article reported multiple results, all results within that single article were combined into
one metric so that the meta-analysis was balanced across all studies.
    We performed a sensitivity analysis of our articles by using the leave-one-out
method (i.e., deleting one study at a time and repeating the analysis) to assess the
stability of the meta-analysis. We used a Q-test to examine whether the true effect size
(ES) varied between studies when a random effect was applied (i.e., heterogeneity,
Tufanaru et al., 2015). A signiﬁcant Q-value reﬂected heterogeneity between samples.
In addition, the I2 statistic indicated different levels of heterogeneity at 25% (low
degree), 50% (moderate degree), and 75% (high degree) (Higgins et al., 2003). We used
I2 to interpret the magnitude of heterogeneity for signiﬁcant Q-values.
    Publication bias is common in meta-analysis because unpublished articles, often
with null effects, are excluded from such analysis. We evaluated publication bias with
the Fail-safe number (N, Nf.s) test (Field & Gillett, 2010) and Funnel Plot (Verhagen &
Ferreira, 2014). A relatively high fail-safe number indicates publication bias. We used a
forest plot to represent the ES and 95% conﬁdence intervals (CIs) to indicate the
correlation between the two variables (Marks-Anglin et al., 2021). We adopted
McGrath and Meyer’s suggestion that values of .37, .24, and .10 represent large,
medium, and small ES. The ES was considered statistically signiﬁcant at the p <
.05 level if the CI did not include zero.

Results
Descriptions of Study Characteristics
The included 19 studies were published between January 2000 and September 2023.
These articles were conducted in four different continents: eleven in Europe (Sweden =
3; Norway = 2; Netherlands = 2; Britian = 1, Denmark = 1; and Germany = 2); three in
America (USA = 2; and Jamaica = 1); three in Oceania (Australia = 2; and New
Zealand = 1), and two in Asia (Korea = 1; and Hong Kong = 1). These articles included
a total of 4156 participants, of whom 1837 were adolescents, and 2319 were adults (see
Table 2). Further, we found eight studies sampled elite athletes as participants, while
eleven sampled non-elite athletes as participants. Furthermore, 14 studies could be
classiﬁed as contact sports, three as non-contact sports, and two as mixed. Seven studies
used sport-speciﬁc measures of stressors, ﬁve studies used general stress measures, and
seven studies used mixed measures of stressors.


Heterogeneity Analysis
The meta-analysis of these 19 studies indicated signiﬁcant heterogeneity with a Q-value
of Q(18) = 106.71 (p < .001) and an I2 value of 83.13, indicating a medium level of
heterogeneity. This moderate heterogeneity can be attributed to the data or design, such
as differences in study populations, targeted effects, survey recruitment, administration
methods, and many others. Therefore, we adopted a random-effects model and con-
ducted a further moderation analysis.


Sensitivity Analysis
Sensitivity analysis determines the robustness of each article’s contribution to the
overall results. We removed one study at a time from the analysis to determine the
change in overall ES when that article was removed. Our sensitivity analysis revealed
that the exclusion of studies individually led to I2 values ranging from 78.37 to 84.07,
showing little change (values all fall into large heterogeneity), compared with the
overall analysis I2 value of 83.13, conﬁrming that each separate study contributed about
equally to these stable results.


Publication Bias
Although the Funnel Plots indicated a degree of asymmetry (Figure 2), this method has
always been controversial because judging the symmetry of the subjective visual graph
with only a few articles can be difﬁcult. Thus, we used the Fail-safe Number test and
found a Z-value of 8.20 (p < .001), indicating no publication bias. The number of

574	Discussion
575	By adopting Anserson and Williams’s (1998) stress-injury model, we systemically
576	reviewed and conducted a meta-analysis for moderate-quality research published over a
577	23-year period between 2000 and 2023. We found the relationship between lifetime
578	stress history and sport injury statistically signiﬁcant but small in effect size (r = .12).
579	
580	
581	
582	
583	Figure 6. Meta-Analysis of All 19 Studies Investigating the Effect between Stress and Athletic
584	Injury (Group by Nature of Sports).
585	 Chyi et al.                                                                                17
586	
587	
588	
589	
590	Figure 7. Meta-Analysis of All 19 Studies Investigating the Effect between Stress and Athletic
591	Injury (Group by Stress Measurement).
592	
593	
594	Further, this relationship was moderated by: (a) athletes’ age (with the relationship
595	stronger in adults than adolescents); (b) athletes’ region (with the relationship stronger
596	in the Americas, Asia, and Oceana than in Europe); (c) sport-type (with the relationship
597	stronger in contact than non-contact sports); (d) stress measurement scale type (with the
598	relationship stronger on non-speciﬁc measures than sport-speciﬁc measures); and (e)
599	athlete competition level (with the relationship stronger among non-elite than elite
600	athletes). These initial ﬁndings provide several implications for researchers and
601	practitioners.
602	
603	
604	Theoretical Contributions and Implications
605	First, our results conﬁrmed the overall presence of a signiﬁcant stress history-sport
606	injury relationship, supporting recent investigators’ reports (Li et al., 2019; Pensgaard
607	et al., 2017) while also conﬁrming Ivarsson et al.’s (2017) report that the effect size of
608	this stress history - sport injury relationship is small (Ivarsson et al., 2017). While our
609	results differ from some investigators’ conclusions (e.g., Maddison & Prapavessis,
610	2005) that there is no relationship between the history of stressors and sport injury, it is
611	to be expected that this small effect size ﬁnding may be present in some studies and not
612	others. This disparity may be explained in part by varying research designs (e.g., using
613	injury time-loss as a criterion) or by different investigators having designs that em-
614	phasized different aspects of the ﬁve signiﬁcant moderating effects detailed above, as,
615	for example, a contact or non-contact type of sport (e.g., ballet, running). Future
616	 18                                                         Perceptual and Motor Skills 0(0)
617	
618	
619	
620	
621	Figure 8. Meta-Analysis of All 19 Studies Investigating the Effect between Stress and Athletic
622	Injury (Group by Competition Level).
623	
624	
625	investigators should carefully consider and then discuss which moderating variables
626	they wish to emphasize and why.
627	    Our provision of quantiﬁed evidence on how the stress history – sport injury re-
628	lationship might be moderated can be particularly valuable to researchers going for-
629	ward. Theoretically, stressors are stimuli that exist naturally in the environment (Taylor,
630	2010). Yet, in sports settings, there are both sport-speciﬁc stresses (e.g., performance
631	demands, training, competition adaptation, coach-athlete relationship, injury) and
632	general life stress (e.g., family relationships, romantic relationships, and interpersonal
633	relationships). For college student-athletes, academic demands can be major stressors
634	(Lu et al., 2012). Not only are these important at the group level (as we studied in this
635	meta-analysis), but they may be particularly important at the level of individual
636	athletes. Our ﬁnding that non-speciﬁc stresses may be particularly inﬂuential to later
637	sport injury is a potent reminder to coaches interested in protecting their players from
638	injury to attend to stresses in an athlete’s general life experience. Since, over the long
639	term, researchers contend that heightened stress may lead to distracted attention and
640	muscle tension, which, in turn, leads to accidents during sports training and competition
641	(Appaneal & Habif, 2013), sports professionals should help athletes manage their life
642	stressors to reduce sport injury (Ivarsson et al., 2017).
643	    Further, since competitive sports have unique cultures with embedded diverse
644	stressors that include team and culture, selection, logistics and operations, and coaching
645	(Arnold et al., 2013) as well as burnout (Lin et al., 2022), substance abuse (de Grace
646	et al., 2017), and mental health concerns (Rice et al., 2016), practitioners, coaches, and
647	 Chyi et al.                                                                             19
648	
649	sports professionals must manage athletes’ stressors to help athletes train and compete
650	in a safe and protective environment.
651	    Our discovery of a small ES in the stress history/sport injury relationship may be
652	explained in several ways. First, in highly competitive modern sports contexts, many
653	well-trained professionals, such as sports psychologists, physical therapists, and sports
654	ofﬁcials, offer stress management programs for athletes to protect them from stress-
655	related illness, depression, or burnout. Athletes may learn diverse coping skills to
656	handle life stressors during training and daily living to attenuate the effect of stressors
657	on physical and mental well-being. Fortunately, some (perhaps particularly elite)
658	athletes may have accumulated important coping experiences to content with stress,
659	lowering their risk for subsequent injury. In keeping with Williams and Andersen’s
660	(1998) proposal that psychosocial variables might moderate the stress history - sport
661	injury relationship, these authors also suggested that psychological intervention might
662	moderate it as well by reducing its strength. In fact, Galante et al. (2018) randomly
663	assigned 616 UK college students to Mindfulness Skills for Students (MSS) training
664	and found that this MSS training increased resilience and reduced stress compared to a
665	control group.
666	    Similarly, Cohen et al. contended that social support can buffer the effects of
667	environmental stress. Thus, different personal or psychosocial factors inﬂuence this
668	relationship in a dynamic, bi-directional fashion, opening a wide pathway for further
669	study. Finally, the sample size of the included studies might have inﬂuenced effect size
670	(i.e., if studies recruited large samples, statistical power and effect sizes would be
671	increased). According to Sink and Mvududu (2010), the sample size, effect size, and
672	statistical power will inﬂuence each other when conducting any research.
673	    Regarding our discovery that the ES for the stress history/sport injury relationship
674	was larger for adults than for adolescents, Lin et al. (2022) drew similar conclusions
675	from their systematic review and meta-analysis comparing athletes’ stress and burnout.
676	They too found that older athletes (age 19–22) had a higher ES in this in this rela-
677	tionship than did adolescent athletes (age 13–18). According to sports talent devel-
678	opment theory (Pankow et al., 2021), as athletes mature, they must engage in more
679	intensive training and competition, with increasing challenges and difﬁculties. Our data
680	remind us that, beyond these sport speciﬁc stresses, older athletes may also face greater
681	non-speciﬁc stress, especially of a cumulative nature.
682	    The moderating effect of participants’ home regions on the stress history/sport injury
683	relationship is interesting and requires much more study to fully understand. Effect size
684	differences were small but signiﬁcant between America, Asia, and Oceania (higher
685	stress history -sport injury relationships) and Europe. Participants’ region encapsulates
686	complex ethnic and cultural differences that may inﬂuence sports’ popularity, de-
687	velopment, and management (Jarvie, 2013) and important non-speciﬁc stress levels.
688	Perhaps it is important that sports participation in Europe is developed, organized, and
689	practiced in local clubs, whereas in the United States, sport resides in schools, colleges,
690	and universities. Or maybe there is importance in the idea that the United States has
691	more early professionalized and commercialized sports than Europe or that sports
692	 20                                                       Perceptual and Motor Skills 0(0)
693	
694	competitions in Europe have international/global appeal and are governed by non-proﬁt
695	federations while, in the United States, professional sports are national in scope and
696	proﬁt-oriented.48 These complex variables and others will require considerable further
697	research to understand.
698	   Perhaps easiest to understand is our ﬁnding that the stress history/sport injury
699	relationship is stronger for contact than non-contact sports. Contact sports such as
700	soccer, basketball, rugby, and wrestling have the highest injury rates (Backx et al.,
701	1989; Engebretsen et al., 2010), through which to express this relationship. Clearly, a
702	great deal of past research shows that athletes, coaches, referees, physical therapists,
703	and association ofﬁcials should work together to address this problem in contact sports
704	where injury levels are highest, including by changing sport rules to reduce behavior in
705	a competition that is associated with the highest sport injury incidence and by providing
706	appropriate equipment to prevent sport injury (Verhagen et al., 2010).
707	   As already discussed, our ﬁnding of a moderating effect of the type of stress
708	measurement scale on the stress history/sport injury relationship proved valuable in
709	actually measuring differences non-sport-speciﬁc and sport-speciﬁc stress. The sport-
710	speciﬁc measures of stressors used in the studies were reviewed included, for example,
711	the Life Events Survey for Collegiate Athletes (Petrie, 1992), while non-sport-speciﬁc
712	measures developed for the general population included the Hassle and Uplift Scale
713	(HUS; DeLongis, 1988). Future investigators may want to select both or just one of
714	these instruments to concentrate on the type of stress that matters most to a given
715	research question.
716	   Our ﬁnding of a moderation effect based on the athlete’s competition level (elite vs.
717	non-elite) was instructive in that the stress history/sport injury relationship was
718	strongest for the non-elite group, perhaps because elite athletes possessed better
719	psychological skills than non-elite athletes (Mahoney et al., 1987). To become better
720	athletes, they must engage in rigorous physical and skill training and psychological
721	skills training (PST) programs or stress management. Further research is needed to
722	afﬁrm a hypothesis that there can be an insulating or immunizing beneﬁt to the
723	provision of stress management training (perhaps as opposed to a naturalistic tendency
724	for elite athletes to possess more of this resilient capability than others), but our data
725	here are important to highlight the need for those investigations.
726	
727	Limitations and Directions for Future Research
728	Among several limitations of this study, we only included research published in English
729	and excluded research in other languages. Whether our results can be generalized to
730	non-English speaking athletes needs further examination. Further, we only included
731	those studies that examined the stress history-sport injury relationships, and these
732	results may be different from studies that focused on other inter-relationships, such as
733	those between coping resources (e.g., personality and intervention training) and sport
734	injury. Furthermore, the studies we included illustrate the r-value or R2 in the stress-
735	hisotoy - sport injury relationship, ignoring more detailed relationships with different
736	 Chyi et al.                                                                                     21
737	
738	levels of stress or injury severity. There is clearly ample room for follow-on inves-
739	tigators to extend these ﬁndings.
740	   Also, because of insufﬁcient information from some included studies, we did not
741	examine other potential moderating variables, such as gender, duration of sports in-
742	volvement, training intensity, cultural differences, and psychological resilience. We
743	suggest that future investigators examine whether these variables might also moderate
744	the stress history - sport injury relationship. Speciﬁcally, Galli and Gonzalez (2015)
745	argued that psychological resilience has an advantage in buffering stress from sub-
746	sequent adversity (e.g., sport injury). Whether athletes high in psychological resilience
747	react better than their counterparts in stressful situations needs further examination, and
748	efforts to demonstrate that resilience can be enhanced would be particularly valuable.
749	Similarly, culture plays an important role in cognition, emotion, and motivation
750	(Atkinson, 1985); and its further study, while particularly complex, is needed.
751	
752	
753	Conclusion
754	Sport injury is both prevalent and broadly impactful for years to come to athletes’
755	physical and psychological well-being. There is an important and sometimes confusing
756	relationship between a lifetime history of stress and sport injury. In this systematic
757	review and meta-analysis, we afﬁrmed that this relationship is statistically signiﬁcant,
758	even small in its effect size, and we identiﬁed and discussed a set of important
759	moderating variables that may help account for variable ﬁndings and effect sizes in this
760	important dynamic, and sometimes bi-directional inter-relationship.
761	
762	Declaration of Conﬂicting Interests
763	The author(s) declared no potential conﬂicts of interest with respect to the research, authorship,
764	and/or publication of this article.
765	
766	
767	Funding
768	The author(s) received no ﬁnancial support for the research, authorship, and/or publication of this
769	article.
770	
771	
772	ORCID iDs
773	Frank J. H. Lu  https://orcid.org/0000-0002-2613-6948

explained in several ways. First, in highly competitive modern sports contexts, many
well-trained professionals, such as sports psychologists, physical therapists, and sports
ofﬁcials, offer stress management programs for athletes to protect them from stress-
related illness, depression, or burnout. Athletes may learn diverse coping skills to
handle life stressors during training and daily living to attenuate the effect of stressors
on physical and mental well-being. Fortunately, some (perhaps particularly elite)
athletes may have accumulated important coping experiences to content with stress,
lowering their risk for subsequent injury. In keeping with Williams and Andersen’s
(1998) proposal that psychosocial variables might moderate the stress history - sport
injury relationship, these authors also suggested that psychological intervention might
moderate it as well by reducing its strength. In fact, Galante et al. (2018) randomly
assigned 616 UK college students to Mindfulness Skills for Students (MSS) training
and found that this MSS training increased resilience and reduced stress compared to a
control group.
    Similarly, Cohen et al. contended that social support can buffer the effects of
environmental stress. Thus, different personal or psychosocial factors inﬂuence this
relationship in a dynamic, bi-directional fashion, opening a wide pathway for further
study. Finally, the sample size of the included studies might have inﬂuenced effect size
(i.e., if studies recruited large samples, statistical power and effect sizes would be
increased). According to Sink and Mvududu (2010), the sample size, effect size, and
statistical power will inﬂuence each other when conducting any research.
    Regarding our discovery that the ES for the stress history/sport injury relationship
was larger for adults than for adolescents, Lin et al. (2022) drew similar conclusions
from their systematic review and meta-analysis comparing athletes’ stress and burnout.
They too found that older athletes (age 19–22) had a higher ES in this in this rela-
tionship than did adolescent athletes (age 13–18). According to sports talent devel-
opment theory (Pankow et al., 2021), as athletes mature, they must engage in more
intensive training and competition, with increasing challenges and difﬁculties. Our data
remind us that, beyond these sport speciﬁc stresses, older athletes may also face greater
non-speciﬁc stress, especially of a cumulative nature.
    The moderating effect of participants’ home regions on the stress history/sport injury
relationship is interesting and requires much more study to fully understand. Effect size
differences were small but signiﬁcant between America, Asia, and Oceania (higher
stress history -sport injury relationships) and Europe. Participants’ region encapsulates
complex ethnic and cultural differences that may inﬂuence sports’ popularity, de-
velopment, and management (Jarvie, 2013) and important non-speciﬁc stress levels.
Perhaps it is important that sports participation in Europe is developed, organized, and
practiced in local clubs, whereas in the United States, sport resides in schools, colleges,
and universities. Or maybe there is importance in the idea that the United States has
more early professionalized and commercialized sports than Europe or that sports
 20                                                       Perceptual and Motor Skills 0(0)

competitions in Europe have international/global appeal and are governed by non-proﬁt
federations while, in the United States, professional sports are national in scope and
proﬁt-oriented.48 These complex variables and others will require considerable further
research to understand.
   Perhaps easiest to understand is our ﬁnding that the stress history/sport injury
relationship is stronger for contact than non-contact sports. Contact sports such as
soccer, basketball, rugby, and wrestling have the highest injury rates (Backx et al.,
1989; Engebretsen et al., 2010), through which to express this relationship. Clearly, a
great deal of past research shows that athletes, coaches, referees, physical therapists,
and association ofﬁcials should work together to address this problem in contact sports
where injury levels are highest, including by changing sport rules to reduce behavior in
a competition that is associated with the highest sport injury incidence and by providing
appropriate equipment to prevent sport injury (Verhagen et al., 2010).
   As already discussed, our ﬁnding of a moderating effect of the type of stress
measurement scale on the stress history/sport injury relationship proved valuable in
actually measuring differences non-sport-speciﬁc and sport-speciﬁc stress. The sport-
speciﬁc measures of stressors used in the studies were reviewed included, for example,
the Life Events Survey for Collegiate Athletes (Petrie, 1992), while non-sport-speciﬁc
measures developed for the general population included the Hassle and Uplift Scale
(HUS; DeLongis, 1988). Future investigators may want to select both or just one of
these instruments to concentrate on the type of stress that matters most to a given
research question.
   Our ﬁnding of a moderation effect based on the athlete’s competition level (elite vs.
non-elite) was instructive in that the stress history/sport injury relationship was
strongest for the non-elite group, perhaps because elite athletes possessed better
psychological skills than non-elite athletes (Mahoney et al., 1987). To become better
athletes, they must engage in rigorous physical and skill training and psychological
skills training (PST) programs or stress management. Further research is needed to
afﬁrm a hypothesis that there can be an insulating or immunizing beneﬁt to the
provision of stress management training (perhaps as opposed to a naturalistic tendency
for elite athletes to possess more of this resilient capability than others), but our data
here are important to highlight the need for those investigations.

Limitations and Directions for Future Research
Among several limitations of this study, we only included research published in English
and excluded research in other languages. Whether our results can be generalized to
non-English speaking athletes needs further examination. Further, we only included
those studies that examined the stress history-sport injury relationships, and these
results may be different from studies that focused on other inter-relationships, such as
those between coping resources (e.g., personality and intervention training) and sport
injury. Furthermore, the studies we included illustrate the r-value or R2 in the stress-
hisotoy - sport injury relationship, ignoring more detailed relationships with different
 Chyi et al.                                                                                     21

levels of stress or injury severity. There is clearly ample room for follow-on inves-
tigators to extend these ﬁndings.
   Also, because of insufﬁcient information from some included studies, we did not
examine other potential moderating variables, such as gender, duration of sports in-
volvement, training intensity, cultural differences, and psychological resilience. We
suggest that future investigators examine whether these variables might also moderate
the stress history - sport injury relationship. Speciﬁcally, Galli and Gonzalez (2015)
argued that psychological resilience has an advantage in buffering stress from sub-
sequent adversity (e.g., sport injury). Whether athletes high in psychological resilience
react better than their counterparts in stressful situations needs further examination, and
efforts to demonstrate that resilience can be enhanced would be particularly valuable.
Similarly, culture plays an important role in cognition, emotion, and motivation
(Atkinson, 1985); and its further study, while particularly complex, is needed.


Conclusion
Sport injury is both prevalent and broadly impactful for years to come to athletes’
physical and psychological well-being. There is an important and sometimes confusing
relationship between a lifetime history of stress and sport injury. In this systematic
review and meta-analysis, we afﬁrmed that this relationship is statistically signiﬁcant,
even small in its effect size, and we identiﬁed and discussed a set of important
moderating variables that may help account for variable ﬁndings and effect sizes in this
important dynamic, and sometimes bi-directional inter-relationship.

and/or publication of this article.

article.

Original Research


Relationship Between Cognitive Performance
and Lower Extremity Biomechanics
Implications for Sports-Related Concussion
Jason M. Avedesian,*†‡ PhD, Tracey Covassin,§ PhD, Shelby Baez,§ PhD, ATC,
Jennifer Nash,k PT, DPT, Ed Nagelhout,{ PhD, and Janet S. Dufek,‡ PhD
Investigation performed at Michigan State University, East Lansing, Michigan, USA

Background: Collegiate athletes with prior sports-related concussion (SRC) are at increased risk for lower extremity (LE) injuries;
however, the biomechanical and cognitive mechanisms underlying the SRC-LE injury relationship are not well understood.
Purpose: To examine the association between cognitive performance and LE land-and-cut biomechanics among collegiate
athletes with and without a history of SRC and to determine the association among multiple cognitive testing batteries in the same
athlete cohort.
Study Design: Controlled laboratory study.
Methods: A cohort of 20 collegiate athletes with prior SRC (9 men, 11 women; mean ± standard deviation [SD] age, 20.5 ± 1.3
years; mean ± SD time since last SRC, 461 ± 263 days) and 20 matched controls (9 men, 11 women; mean ± SD age, 19.8 ± 1.3
years) completed land-and-cut tasks using the dominant and nondominant limbs. LE biomechanical variables and a functional
visuomotor reaction time (FVMRT) were collected during each trial. Athletes also completed the Immediate Post-Concussion
Assessment and Cognitive Test (ImPACT) and Senaptec Sensory Station assessments.
Results: In the SRC cohort, Pearson correlation coefficients indicated slower FVMRT was moderately correlated with decreased
dominant limb (r ¼ –0.512) and nondominant limb (r ¼ –0.500) knee flexion, while increased dominant limb knee abduction moment
was moderately correlated with decreased ImPACT Visual Memory score (r ¼ –0.539) and slower ImPACT Reaction Time (r ¼
0.515). Most computerized cognitive measures were not associated with FVMRT in either cohort (P > .05).
Conclusion: Decreased reaction time and working memory performance were moderately correlated with decreased sagittal
plane knee motion and increased frontal plane knee loading in collegiate athletes with a history of SRC. The present findings
suggest a potential unique relationship between cognitive performance and LE neuromuscular control in athletes with a history of
SRC injury. Last, we determined that computerized measures of cognitive performance often utilized for SRC management are
dissimilar to sport-specific cognitive processes.
Clinical Relevance: Understanding the relationship between cognitive performance and LE biomechanics in athletes with prior
SRC may inform future clinical management strategies. Future research should prospectively assess cognitive and biomechanical
measures, along with LE injury incidence, to identify mechanisms underlying the SRC-LE injury relationship.
Keywords: reaction time; visual memory; multiple object tracking; musculoskeletal injury

{
 "id":"Q44",
 "sourceFile":"Relationship between cognitive performance and lower extremity biomechanics - Implications for sports-related concussion.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text ('Relationship Between Cognitive Performance and Lower Extremity Biomechanics: Implications for Sports-Related Concussion') matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Laboratory / Experimental Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Brain Health & Psychology"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Rehabilitation"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Female Athletes","Collegiate","Healthy Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Controlled laboratory study of 20 NCAA Division I athletes with prior sports-related concussion (9 men, 11 women; mean 461 days since last concussion, all clinically cleared) and 20 controls matched by sport, position, sex and age. Participants performed unanticipated land-and-cut tasks while lower extremity biomechanics and a functional visuomotor reaction time were recorded, and completed ImPACT and Senaptec cognitive tests. In the concussion group, slower functional reaction time was moderately correlated with reduced knee flexion, and larger dominant-limb knee abduction moment was moderately correlated with lower ImPACT Visual Memory (r = -0.539) and with ImPACT Reaction Time (r = 0.515).",
 "screeningLimitations":"Twenty athletes per group, a single cross-sectional session and many correlations tested without correction mean several significant findings could be chance. Correlations were run separately within each group and many did not differ between groups, and no injury outcomes were measured, so the study cannot show that cognitive deficits cause riskier mechanics or injury.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read this as showing that poor cognitive scores after concussion predict knee injury; the study measured correlations with laboratory mechanics in 40 athletes and recorded no injuries.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2021,
   "citation":"Avedesian JM, Covassin T, Baez S, Nash J, Nagelhout E, Dufek JS. Relationship Between Cognitive Performance and Lower Extremity Biomechanics: Implications for Sports-Related Concussion. Orthop J Sports Med. 2021;9(8):23259671211032246.",
   "doi":"10.1177/23259671211032246",
   "abstract":"In 20 collegiate athletes with prior sports-related concussion and 20 matched controls, slower functional visuomotor reaction time was correlated with reduced knee flexion, and greater dominant-limb knee abduction moment was correlated with poorer ImPACT visual memory and ImPACT reaction time in the concussion group. Most computerised cognitive measures were not associated with the functional reaction time.",
   "tldr":"In athletes with a prior concussion, slower reaction time and poorer visual memory went with knee mechanics linked to injury risk during cutting. Standard computerised concussion tests did not track the sport-specific reaction measure well.",
   "methods":"Controlled laboratory study with a single testing session. Twenty NCAA Division I athletes with physician-diagnosed collegiate concussion (9 men, 11 women) and 20 matched controls from seven sports completed unanticipated land-and-cut tasks on dominant and non-dominant limbs, with motion capture and force plates over the first 100 ms of contact and a light-cued functional visuomotor reaction time. Athletes also completed ImPACT and three Senaptec Sensory Station tasks, and Pearson correlations were run for all athletes and for each group.",
   "findings":"In the concussion group, slower functional reaction time was moderately correlated with reduced dominant-limb knee flexion (r = -0.514) and slower non-dominant reaction time with reduced non-dominant knee flexion (r = -0.500). Increased dominant-limb knee abduction moment was moderately correlated with lower ImPACT Visual Memory (r = -0.539) and ImPACT Reaction Time (r = 0.515), and Go/No Go score with non-dominant vGRF (r = -0.700). Apart from MOT, computerised cognitive measures were not associated with functional reaction time in any cohort, and some correlations seen in controls were absent in the concussion group.",
   "limitations":"Small sample of 20 per group, cross-sectional, with many uncorrected correlations. Pre-collegiate concussion history, ADHD status and the reliability of the functional reaction time and Senaptec measures were not addressed, and mean time since concussion was 461 days. The abstract gives r = -0.512 for dominant knee flexion (table and text: -0.514; -0.512 is knee extension moment) and calls the ImPACT reaction time finding 'slower' where the results text says 'faster'; this record uses the table values.",
   "practicalImplications":"Reaction time and working memory may be worth assessing alongside landing and cutting mechanics in athletes with a concussion history. Computerised concussion tests alone may not reflect sport-specific cognitive processing.",
   "athleteDev":"In athletes with a prior concussion, poorer reaction time and visual memory were related to knee mechanics during cutting, which supports pairing cognitive and movement screening when profiling these athletes. The data do not show that training either one changes the other.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot be used to clear an athlete to return to sport. Its sample was already cleared and a mean of 461 days post-concussion, and it was not designed to test readiness to return after an acute injury."
 },
 "verification":{
   "status":"CORRECTED",
   "changes":[
     "findings: dominant knee flexion r = -0.512 (abstract) -> r = -0.514 per Table 3 and results text ('decreased dominant limb knee flexion (r = -0.514; P = .024)'); abstract conflict noted in limitations",
     "findings/abstract/evidenceSummary: 'slower ImPACT Reaction Time' -> direction stated neutrally (r = 0.515) because results text says 'faster Reaction Time was moderately correlated with increased dominant limb knee abduction moment'",
     "populations: 'Injured Athletes' -> 'Healthy Athletes'; concussion group was clinically cleared ('All athletes in the present study were clinically cleared for sports and were well beyond 2 months post-SRC') and LE-injured athletes were excluded",
     "screeningLimitations: 'correlations were reported within the concussion group' -> correlations were run for all athletes and each group, many did not differ between groups; added multiple-testing and no injury outcomes",
     "synthesisCaution: reframed around absence of injury outcomes",
     "limitations: added authors' limits (pre-collegiate SRC not collected, ADHD not excluded, reliability of FVMRT and Senaptec unknown)"
   ],
   "residualConcerns":"Health-status tag is a judgment call: the exposure group had prior concussions but were cleared and symptom status is not reported. Abstract and results disagree on the direction label for ImPACT Reaction Time.",
   "spotCheckPriority":"high"
 }
}

 Fatigue can be measured through internal and external loads [5]. In football, there are
 several internal load methods that are very popular to measure fatigue and response to

 Conversely, there are some physical tests that can help to check the current physical
 condition of the athletes through external loads. It has been evidenced that velocity loss
 is a reliable marker of neuromuscular fatigue, which is described as a decrease in the
 physical and mental functions [11]. This is why most of the scientific literature has used
 the repeated sprint ability (RSA) test to measure fatigue, especially in team sports such as
 football; this is because RSA and the ability to exercise at high intensity are key capacities

 statistical analysis.
 2.4.3. Repeated Sprint Ability (RSA)
 The RSA test included six sprints of 30 m with 20 s recovery between sprints. Two
 pairs of photocells (Witty, Microgate, Bolzano, Italy), placed at 0 and 30 m, were used. The
 following measures were calculated: sprint time (RSAt), best sprint time, average time,
 total time, percentage difference between the first and the rest of the sprints during the RSA
 test − %Diff − [((sprint time − first sprint time)/first sprint time) × 100] and percentage
 difference between the best and the rest of the sprints during the RSA test − %Best −
 [((sprint time − best time)/best time) × 100]. The previous two sprints performed during
 the warm-up were used as a control measure to ensure that players performed the RSA test
 at maximum speed. If the time of the first RSA test sprint was longer (>5%) than the best
 individual sprint performed before the start of the test, the RSA test was not considered
 valid, and the player had to repeat the test after 5 min of recovery.

 the variables was confirmed by histogram charts and the Shapiro–Wilk distribution test.
 A mixed two-way analysis of variance was performed to analyse the effect of the level of

 asymmetry group was used as an independent factor, and the sprint number as a repeated
 measured factor to control the interaction of the thermal asymmetry group with the sprint
 progression. Bonferroni post hoc pairwise comparisons were undertaken to compare the

65	 Fatigue can be measured through internal and external loads [5]. In football, there are
66	 several internal load methods that are very popular to measure fatigue and response to
67	 exercise; however, most of them present some disadvantages, so they should be combined
68	 with other methods. Heart rate measurements are the most common, but they are imprecise
69	 in high-intensity actions and sprints, which are crucial aspects of football [8]. Blood and
70	 bone markers are more precise, but they are difficult to extract on a weekly basis (price
71	 and time), and some players can feel uncomfortable being exposed continuously to them.
72	 Therefore, extracting them whenever the physical status of the player needs to be known
73	 can be unsustainable during regular-season training [9]. Questionnaires are very simple to
74	 administer but particularly subjective, introducing a high risk of bias [10].
75	 Conversely, there are some physical tests that can help to check the current physical
76	 condition of the athletes through external loads. It has been evidenced that velocity loss
77	 is a reliable marker of neuromuscular fatigue, which is described as a decrease in the
78	 physical and mental functions [11]. This is why most of the scientific literature has used
79	 the repeated sprint ability (RSA) test to measure fatigue, especially in team sports such as
80	 football; this is because RSA and the ability to exercise at high intensity are key capacities
81	 for optimal performance, and a decreased sprint repetition capacity is a good indicator
82	 of fatigue in sports [12]. However, this method can lack precision in some situations, as
83	 the scientific literature has found that sprint performance can be maintained in situations
84	 of neuromuscular fatigue after match play [13]. This is why some coaches incorporate a
85	 stretching–shortening movement, such as a countermovement jump (CMJ) to detect fatigue,
86	 as it can highlight impairments in jump performance between two events [14]; a good
87	 relationship between sprint ability and CMJ capacity has been verified [14].
88	 Therefore, scientific evidence has shown CMJ performance to be an objective marker
89	 of fatigue and supercompensation, as neuromuscular fatigue has been associated with a
90	 decrease in the average CMJ height [15], causing this method to be used frequently to assess
91	 neuromuscular fatigue [16]. However, when using RSA to assess neuromuscular fatigue,
92	 the number of sprints induces great variability between athletes [17]. In addition, when
93	 using CMJs, it is important to consider that the same fatiguing stimuli can elicit different
94	 effects between individuals, and sometimes athletes can adjust their jumping strategy
95	 to maintain their performance [18]. Moreover, players’ need to exert maximal effort to
96	 measure fatigue is not optimal, as this effort increases injury risk. Hence, the use of other
97	 technologies which can provide information and help coaches without the need to perform
98	 a physical test, can be considered. In this sense, one option is infrared thermography (IRT),

100	 physiological variables through the control of the skin temperature [19].

441	 difference between the best and the rest of the sprints during the RSA test − %Best −
442	 [((sprint time − best time)/best time) × 100]. The previous two sprints performed during
