614	 4. Discussion
615	 The purpose of this study was to determine if there is a relationship between thermal
616	 asymmetries provided by thermography and performance in a repeated sprint ability (RSA)
617	 test and in countermovement jumps (CMJs) before and after the RSA test. The results of the
618	 RSA test showed a significant interaction between hamstring asymmetry and the number
619	 of sprints in the RSAt and in the % Diff. The hamstring high-asymmetry group showed a
620	 higher %Diff in sprint 2, which means that there is a significative longer time with respect
621	 Sensors 2023, 23, 631 7 of 9
622	 to sprint 1 (worse performance) than in the low-asymmetry group. On the other hand,
623	 the hamstring low-asymmetry group reported a higher %Best in sprints 2, 3 and 4. The
624	 cause of this difference in the hamstring %Best may be attributable to the fact that the
625	 low-asymmetry group had the best sprint, which was very fast; therefore, the following best
626	 ones have a significant difference (worse). On the other hand, no differences were found in
627	 the thigh and calf groups for any variable. The reason why the only thermal asymmetry that
628	 influenced the performance was that of hamstrings could be their importance in sprinting,
629	 as they play a crucial role in generating force in the propulsive part of the sprint [28]
630	 and are clearly the most frequently injured muscle during sprinting [4]. The majority of
631	 hamstring muscle injuries occur while the athlete is running at maximal or close to maximal
632	 speeds [29] Many investigations have measured hamstring activity during sprinting with
633	 electromyographic (EMG), and found that the hamstrings are active from the middle of
634	 the swing to the final stance Some of these studies have reported that peak activity occurs
635	 during terminal swing [30], whereas others have found it to occur during stance [31]. Proof
636	 of the effort that these muscles exert in the sprint is that an increase in running speed of
637	 80–100% is linked with an increase in net hamstring muscle force and energy absorption of
638	 1.4 and 1.9 times, respectively [32]. However, this study took data from athletes running on
639	 a treadmill, and the mechanical properties of treadmill surfaces are different from those
640	 of the surfaces on which the athletes usually train and compete (e.g., artificial turf or an
641	 athletic track) [33]. This factor may influence running anatomy, so the results should be
642	 interpreted with caution.
643	 Regarding the CMJ results, the low thermal asymmetry hamstring group has signif-
644	 icantly higher values in the CMJ post-RSA, while in the calf and thigh groups, there are
645	 no significant differences in either CMJ pre- or CMJ post-RSA. Thus, the high thermal
646	 asymmetry hamstring group’s performance was similar to that of the low thermal asym-
647	 metry hamstring group before the RSA, and then its performance decreased in the CMJ
648	 post-RSA. This can be indicative of fatigue, as a decreased average CMJ jump height can
649	 indicate neuromuscular fatigue [34]. The reason why significant differences are only found
650	 in the high-asymmetry hamstring group (and not in the calf and thigh groups) may be that
651	 hamstrings are the most implicated and frequently injured group in sprinting [28], while
652	 calves and thighs seem to play a less crucial role in sprinting; therefore, asymmetry takes
653	 longer to turn into fatigue when performing an RSA test, as they are less implicated in
654	 this activity.
655	 Although the results of this study seem to provide evidence in terms of using and
656	 interpreting thermography to assess RSA and CMJ performance in elite football players,
657	 the results must be interpreted with caution, as certain limitations should be considered.
658	 First, thermography was carried out in just one session; applying thermography in a higher
659	 number of sessions would allow us to corroborate the results of the study. Second, a low
660	 asymmetry cut point was established, and settling a higher asymmetry cut point would
661	 probably show stronger correlations. Finally, the sample was very small, so future research
662	 should be carried out to look for evidence and to check whether these results apply to
663	 different genders, ages and competitive levels.
664	 From a practical point of view, if football coaches can access the thermographs of their
665	 players, they should focus especially on hamstrings (rather than calves and thighs) and
666	 modify the training if necessary. These muscles appear to be the ones with more influence
667	 on the test results, as they are the only ones for which thermal asymmetry of over 0.2 ◦ C
668	 had an effect.
669	 5. Conclusions
670	 Thermography can provide information about performance in CMJ and RSA tests for
671	 hamstring asymmetries over 0.2 ◦ C; meanwhile, calf and thigh asymmetries over 0.2 ◦ C do
672	 not seem to have a relationship with performance in these tests. In short, thermography
673	 results have some correlation with CMJ and RSA performance, but stablishing higher cut
674	 off points would probably allow us to find stronger correlations for hamstring asymmetries,
675	 Sensors 2023, 23, 631 8 of 9
676	 and maybe some correlation for calf and thigh asymmetries which would be helpful for
677	 coaches and athletes.

 Fatigue can be measured through internal and external loads [5]. In football, there are
 several internal load methods that are very popular to measure fatigue and response to
 exercise; however, most of them present some disadvantages, so they should be combined
 with other methods. Heart rate measurements are the most common, but they are imprecise
 in high-intensity actions and sprints, which are crucial aspects of football [8]. Blood and
 bone markers are more precise, but they are difficult to extract on a weekly basis (price
 and time), and some players can feel uncomfortable being exposed continuously to them.
 Therefore, extracting them whenever the physical status of the player needs to be known
 can be unsustainable during regular-season training [9]. Questionnaires are very simple to
 administer but particularly subjective, introducing a high risk of bias [10].
 Conversely, there are some physical tests that can help to check the current physical
 condition of the athletes through external loads. It has been evidenced that velocity loss
 is a reliable marker of neuromuscular fatigue, which is described as a decrease in the
 physical and mental functions [11]. This is why most of the scientific literature has used
 the repeated sprint ability (RSA) test to measure fatigue, especially in team sports such as
 football; this is because RSA and the ability to exercise at high intensity are key capacities
 for optimal performance, and a decreased sprint repetition capacity is a good indicator
 of fatigue in sports [12]. However, this method can lack precision in some situations, as
 the scientific literature has found that sprint performance can be maintained in situations
 of neuromuscular fatigue after match play [13]. This is why some coaches incorporate a
 stretching–shortening movement, such as a countermovement jump (CMJ) to detect fatigue,
 as it can highlight impairments in jump performance between two events [14]; a good
 relationship between sprint ability and CMJ capacity has been verified [14].
 Therefore, scientific evidence has shown CMJ performance to be an objective marker
 of fatigue and supercompensation, as neuromuscular fatigue has been associated with a
 decrease in the average CMJ height [15], causing this method to be used frequently to assess
 neuromuscular fatigue [16]. However, when using RSA to assess neuromuscular fatigue,
 the number of sprints induces great variability between athletes [17]. In addition, when
 using CMJs, it is important to consider that the same fatiguing stimuli can elicit different
 effects between individuals, and sometimes athletes can adjust their jumping strategy
 to maintain their performance [18]. Moreover, players’ need to exert maximal effort to
 measure fatigue is not optimal, as this effort increases injury risk. Hence, the use of other
 technologies which can provide information and help coaches without the need to perform
 a physical test, can be considered. In this sense, one option is infrared thermography (IRT),
 which is a non-radiating, contact-free, safe and non-invasive technology that monitors
 physiological variables through the control of the skin temperature [19].
 This technology gauges the correlation between muscle activation and skin tempera-
 ture, as muscle and skin temperature are directly correlated. The information this technol-
 ogy provided is based on the hyperthermic and hypothermic responses of the skin [20], due
 to the fact that thermography is a reliable method to assess skin temperature [21]. Moreover,
 athletes are presumed to keep their thermal pattern constant in baseline conditions, and
 thermal asymmetries in the bilateral body areas (e.g., ankle, knee, hamstring or elbow) are
 linked to factors related to injuries, such as inflammation or secondary trauma, as in normal
 conditions, the temperature of both sides of the bilateral areas should increase equally [22].
 IRT can detect these asymmetries by comparing bilateral body areas, showing potential in-
 jury risk due to incorrect work assimilations provoked by factors such as excessive training,
 poor technique or muscle overload [23].
 The relevance of IRT is that it can detect temperature asymmetries (and consequent
 risks) before other markers such as pain, making this method extraordinarily effective and
 applicable in preventing injuries [23]. If IRT provides coaches with the ability to detect
 impairments in bilateral body areas before pain, it can allow them to modify the training

 2.4.2. Vertical Jumps
 Players completed 2 CMJ tests: (1) after warming up and (2) after the RSA test, with
 some minutes to recover from it. To measure the height of the jumps, infrared technology
 was used (Optojump Next, Microgate, Bolzano, Italy). The participants were already
 familiar with the movement, and they were instructed to undertake it in the most precise
 way, keeping their hands on their hips to eliminate the influence of arm movement on the
 Sensors 2023, 23, 631 5 of 9
 jump performance. Each player performed three jumps before and after the RSA test (with
 2 min of recovery between jumps). The average of the three jumps was calculated for the
 statistical analysis.
 2.4.3. Repeated Sprint Ability (RSA)
 The RSA test included six sprints of 30 m with 20 s recovery between sprints. Two
 pairs of photocells (Witty, Microgate, Bolzano, Italy), placed at 0 and 30 m, were used. The
 following measures were calculated: sprint time (RSAt), best sprint time, average time,
 total time, percentage difference between the first and the rest of the sprints during the RSA
 test − %Diff − [((sprint time − first sprint time)/first sprint time) × 100] and percentage
 difference between the best and the rest of the sprints during the RSA test − %Best −
 [((sprint time − best time)/best time) × 100]. The previous two sprints performed during
 the warm-up were used as a control measure to ensure that players performed the RSA test
 at maximum speed. If the time of the first RSA test sprint was longer (>5%) than the best
 individual sprint performed before the start of the test, the RSA test was not considered
 valid, and the player had to repeat the test after 5 min of recovery.
 2.5. Statistical Analysis
 The data are presented as means ± standard deviations. The normal distribution of
 the variables was confirmed by histogram charts and the Shapiro–Wilk distribution test.
 A mixed two-way analysis of variance was performed to analyse the effect of the level of
 thermal asymmetry on the RSA variables depending on the sprint number. The thermal
 asymmetry group was used as an independent factor, and the sprint number as a repeated
 measured factor to control the interaction of the thermal asymmetry group with the sprint
 progression. Bonferroni post hoc pairwise comparisons were undertaken to compare the
 RSA variables of the two groups of thermal asymmetries in each of the sprints, including
 the confidence interval (95%). The effect size (ES) was calculated for all the inference
 tests using the partial eta squared (ηp2 = ES) value with the following interpretation:
 small (ES = 0.01–0.059); medium (ES = 0.06–0.14); and large effects (ES > 0.14). The level of
 significance was set at p < 0.05 for all the tests, and all the data were statistically analysed
 using SPSS V24.0. (IBM Corp. Released 2016. IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, Version
 24.0. Armonk, NY: IBM Corp.)

 4. Discussion
 The purpose of this study was to determine if there is a relationship between thermal
 asymmetries provided by thermography and performance in a repeated sprint ability (RSA)
 test and in countermovement jumps (CMJs) before and after the RSA test. The results of the
 RSA test showed a significant interaction between hamstring asymmetry and the number
 of sprints in the RSAt and in the % Diff. The hamstring high-asymmetry group showed a
 higher %Diff in sprint 2, which means that there is a significative longer time with respect
 Sensors 2023, 23, 631 7 of 9
 to sprint 1 (worse performance) than in the low-asymmetry group. On the other hand,
 the hamstring low-asymmetry group reported a higher %Best in sprints 2, 3 and 4. The
 cause of this difference in the hamstring %Best may be attributable to the fact that the
 low-asymmetry group had the best sprint, which was very fast; therefore, the following best
 ones have a significant difference (worse). On the other hand, no differences were found in
 the thigh and calf groups for any variable. The reason why the only thermal asymmetry that
 influenced the performance was that of hamstrings could be their importance in sprinting,
 as they play a crucial role in generating force in the propulsive part of the sprint [28]
 and are clearly the most frequently injured muscle during sprinting [4]. The majority of
 hamstring muscle injuries occur while the athlete is running at maximal or close to maximal
 speeds [29] Many investigations have measured hamstring activity during sprinting with
 electromyographic (EMG), and found that the hamstrings are active from the middle of
 the swing to the final stance Some of these studies have reported that peak activity occurs
 during terminal swing [30], whereas others have found it to occur during stance [31]. Proof
 of the effort that these muscles exert in the sprint is that an increase in running speed of
 80–100% is linked with an increase in net hamstring muscle force and energy absorption of
 1.4 and 1.9 times, respectively [32]. However, this study took data from athletes running on
 a treadmill, and the mechanical properties of treadmill surfaces are different from those
 of the surfaces on which the athletes usually train and compete (e.g., artificial turf or an
 athletic track) [33]. This factor may influence running anatomy, so the results should be
 interpreted with caution.
 Regarding the CMJ results, the low thermal asymmetry hamstring group has signif-
 icantly higher values in the CMJ post-RSA, while in the calf and thigh groups, there are
 no significant differences in either CMJ pre- or CMJ post-RSA. Thus, the high thermal
 asymmetry hamstring group’s performance was similar to that of the low thermal asym-
 metry hamstring group before the RSA, and then its performance decreased in the CMJ
 post-RSA. This can be indicative of fatigue, as a decreased average CMJ jump height can
 indicate neuromuscular fatigue [34]. The reason why significant differences are only found
 in the high-asymmetry hamstring group (and not in the calf and thigh groups) may be that
 hamstrings are the most implicated and frequently injured group in sprinting [28], while
 calves and thighs seem to play a less crucial role in sprinting; therefore, asymmetry takes
 longer to turn into fatigue when performing an RSA test, as they are less implicated in
 this activity.
 Although the results of this study seem to provide evidence in terms of using and
 interpreting thermography to assess RSA and CMJ performance in elite football players,
 the results must be interpreted with caution, as certain limitations should be considered.
 First, thermography was carried out in just one session; applying thermography in a higher
 number of sessions would allow us to corroborate the results of the study. Second, a low
 asymmetry cut point was established, and settling a higher asymmetry cut point would
 probably show stronger correlations. Finally, the sample was very small, so future research
 should be carried out to look for evidence and to check whether these results apply to
 different genders, ages and competitive levels.
 From a practical point of view, if football coaches can access the thermographs of their
 players, they should focus especially on hamstrings (rather than calves and thighs) and

 1 Abstract
 2 Background: Quarterbacks (QBs) in American football frequently perform repetitive overhead
 3 throwing, which can lead to shoulder and elbow injuries. Effective control of trunk and pelvic
 4 movements is considered crucial for minimizing shoulder and elbow joint stress during throwing.
 5 The Kerlan–Jobe Orthopedic Clinic (KJOC) score is a self-perceived index of shoulder and elbow
 6 function and level of competition in overhead athletes. However, the relationship between trunk
 7 and pelvic movements during throwing and the KJOC score among QBs remains unclear. This

 9 sequence and the KJOC score.

16 Jo

17 of competition . Correlations between throwing mechanics and KJOC each item and total scores
18 were assessed using Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient.
19 Results: Trunk rotation at MER during 20-yard throws and hip–shoulder separation at SFC during
20 30-yard throws were positively correlated with KJOC Item 3 (rs = 0.709; p = 0.015 and rs = 0.662;
21 p = 0.026, respectively). Pelvic rotation at BR during 30-yard throws showed a positive correlation
22 with KJOC Item 4 (rs = 0.760; p = 0.007).
23 Conclusion: This study suggests a relationship between trunk and pelvic rotational movements

24 during a quarterback’s throw and certain aspects of subjective shoulder and elbow function.

28 American football is a widely popular sport in the United States and has gained significant
29 popularity in Japan. Among the key positions in the sport is the quarterback (QB), who initiates
30 offensive plays by throwing a football, typically weighing between 397 and 425 g, to a teammate.
31

32

 common shoulder injury. In the same study, they also identified medial collateral ligament injuries

 and elbow injuries requiring surgical intervention typically demand a recovery period of

37
 na

39 QBs. Jo
40 The loads placed on quarterbacks’ shoulders and elbows during throwing have been investigated
41 by several researchers.8,14 Fleisig et al8 reported that during the cocking phase, quarterbacks
42 generate a shoulder anterior force of 350 N and an elbow varus torque of 54 Nm, while Rash et al
43 observed a maximum shoulder anterior force of 250 N. These findings indicate that throwing
44 imposes substantial stress on the shoulder and elbow joints. Quarterback throwing is a whole-body
45 motion in which energy produced by the lower limbs and trunk is transmitted to the upper limbs.
46 In overhead sports, it is generally recognized that inadequate kinetic chain function in proximal

47 segments, such as the trunk and pelvis, increases the mechanical load on distal segments, including
48 the shoulder and elbow.3,9 Furthermore, Labbe et al10 further demonstrated, using inertial
49 measurement units, that trunk and pelvic rotation occurs from stride foot contact to ball release,
50 and that efficient energy transfer to the upper limbs requires appropriate rotation of these segments.
51 Collectively, these reports suggest that controlling trunk and pelvic rotation during throwing may
52 help reduce shoulder and elbow loading and support joint function.
53 The Kerlan–Jobe Orthopedic Clinic (KJOC) score is used to evaluate a self-perceived index of
54

{
 "id":"Q46",
 "sourceFile":"Relationship between trunk and pelvic rotation angles during throwing and the Kerlan–Jobe Orthopedic Clinic score in American football quarterbacks.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text ('Relationship between trunk and pelvic rotation angles during throwing and the Kerlan–Jobe Orthopedic Clinic score in American football quarterbacks') matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"medium",
 "studyDesign":"Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Performance"],
 "sports":["American Football"],
 "populations":["Healthy Athletes","Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Cross-sectional study of 11 healthy quarterbacks (age 18 to 36) from one Japanese university team and one club team, each making five maximum-effort throws at 20 and 30 yards. Trunk rotation, pelvic rotation and hip-shoulder separation, measured with a markerless iPad app (PitchAI), were correlated with the self-reported Kerlan-Jobe Orthopedic Clinic (KJOC) shoulder and elbow score. Several positive correlations were found with individual KJOC items, for example trunk rotation at maximum external rotation (20 yards) with item 3 (rs = 0.709) and pelvic rotation at ball release (30 yards) with item 4 (rs = 0.760).",
 "screeningLimitations":"Eleven players is far below the 84 the authors calculated were needed, and many angle-item correlations were tested without correction, so some significant results may be chance. KJOC scores showed a ceiling effect, and the app's validity for quarterback throwing has not been tested.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read these correlations as evidence that a given throwing mechanic protects the shoulder or elbow; the study correlated app-measured angles with a self-reported score in 11 healthy quarterbacks at one time point.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2026,
   "citation":"Aso T, Tamura M, Kaji N, Akiyama S, Maeda T, Takahashi Y, et al. Relationship between trunk and pelvic rotation angles during throwing and the Kerlan–Jobe Orthopedic Clinic score in American football quarterbacks. JSES Int. 2026.",
   "doi":"10.1016/j.jseint.2025.101607",
   "abstract":"In 11 healthy quarterbacks, trunk and pelvic rotation during throwing correlated with specific items of the KJOC shoulder and elbow function score. Significant correlations were positive and moderate to strong, at both the 20- and 30-yard throw distances.",
   "tldr":"Quarterbacks with more trunk and pelvic rotation at key points of the throw reported better scores on some KJOC shoulder and elbow items. This is a very small correlation study with an app-based measure.",
   "methods":"Eleven healthy quarterbacks without prior shoulder or elbow surgery completed five maximum-effort throws at 20 and 30 yards. A side-on iPad video at 240 Hz was analysed with PitchAI, a markerless app, for trunk rotation, pelvic rotation and hip-shoulder separation at stride foot contact, maximum shoulder external rotation and ball release. These angles were correlated with each KJOC item and the total score using Spearman rank correlation.",
   "findings":"At 20 yards, trunk rotation at maximum external rotation correlated with KJOC item 3 on weakness or fatigue (rs = 0.709, p = 0.015). At 30 yards, hip-shoulder separation at stride foot contact correlated with item 3 (rs = 0.662, p = 0.026) and pelvic rotation at ball release with item 4 (rs = 0.760, p = 0.007). Further significant positive correlations were reported for items 5, 7 and 10 (rs = 0.616 to 0.839).",
   "limitations":"Eleven participants from two teams, against an a priori sample size of 84, with many correlations tested. KJOC scores were mostly very high (ceiling effect), and PitchAI has been validated in baseball pitching but not quarterback throwing. Pre-proof article that has not completed copyediting; cross-sectional design in healthy players only.",
   "practicalImplications":"Trunk and pelvic rotation are candidate variables to study in quarterback throwing assessments alongside the KJOC score. The findings do not show which mechanic to change to reduce injury.",
   "athleteDev":"Trunk and pelvic rotation were related to some self-reported shoulder and elbow function items in healthy quarterbacks. This is hypothesis-generating and does not by itself justify changing a quarterback's throwing technique.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It included only healthy quarterbacks and does not test whether throwing mechanics or KJOC scores indicate readiness to return after injury."
 },

     "findings: added further significant correlations with items 5, 7 and 10 reported in results",
     "screeningLimitations/limitations: added a priori sample size of 84, multiple testing, KJOC ceiling effect and unvalidated app for QB throwing ('its validity and reliability for quarterback throwing have not yet been examined')",
     "athleteDev: softened 'supports including trunk and pelvic mechanics in throwing-technique work'",
     "paper.citation: added sixth author Takahashi Y before et al."
   ],
   "residualConcerns":"Pre-proof version; sex of participants not stated. Competition level is mixed (university and club X League players).",
   "spotCheckPriority":"high"
 }
}

 ABSTRACT
 BELLINGER, P., M. N. BOURNE, S. DUHIG, E. LIEVENS, B. KENNEDY, A. MARTIN, C. COOPER, M. TREDREA, H. RICE, W.
 DERAVE, and C. MINAHAN. Relationships between Lower Limb Muscle Characteristics and Force–Velocity Profiles Derived during
 Sprinting and Jumping. Med. Sci. Sports Exerc., Vol. 53, No. 7, pp. 1400–1411, 2021. Purpose: This study aimed to identify the relationships
 between lower limb muscle characteristics and mechanical variables derived from the vertical (jumping) and horizontal (sprinting) force–
 velocity–power (FVP) profiles. Methods: Nineteen subelite male rugby league players performed a series of squat jumps and linear 30-m
 sprints to derive the vertical and horizontal FVP profiles, respectively. The theoretical maximal force (F0), velocity (V0), and power (Pmax)
 were derived from both the vertical (i.e., vF0, vV0, and vPmax) and the horizontal (i.e., hF0, hV0, and hPmax) FVP profiles. Vastus lateralis
 (VL), biceps femoris long head, and gastrocnemius medialis (GM) and lateralis muscle fascicle length, pennation angle, and thickness were
 measured using B-mode ultrasonography. Magnetic resonance imaging was used to calculate volumes of major lower limb muscles, whereas
 proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy was used to quantify the carnosine content of the GM to estimate muscle fiber typology. Results:
 Variation in vPmax was best explained by GM muscle fiber typology (i.e., greater estimated proportion of Type II fibers) and VL volume (ad-
 justed r2 = 0.440, P = 0.006), whereas adductor and vastus medialis volume and GM muscle fiber typology explained the most variation in
APPLIED SCIENCES
 hPmax (adjusted r2 = 0.634, P = 0.032). Rectus femoris and VL volume explained variation in vF0 (r2 = 0.430, P = 0.008), whereas adductor
 and vastus medialis volume explained variation in hF0 (r2 = 0.432, P = 0.007). Variations in vV0 and hV0 were best explained by GM muscle
 fiber typology (adjusted r2 = 0.580, P < 0.001) and GM muscle fiber typology and biceps femoris short head volume (adjusted r2 = 0.590,
 P < 0.001), respectively. Conclusion: Muscle fiber typology and muscle volume are strong determinants of maximal muscle power in jumping
 and sprinting by influencing the velocity- and force-oriented mechanical variables. Key Words: MUSCLE FIBER–TYPE COMPOSITION,

 ABSTRACT
 Approximately 1.6-3.8 million sports-related traumatic brain injuries occur each year in the US. Researchers track
 the head motion using a variety of techniques to study the head injury biomechanics. To understand how helmets
 provide head protection, quantification of the relative motion between the head and the helmet is necessary. The
 purpose of this study was to compare helmet and head kinematics and quantify the relative motion of helmet with
 respect to head during experimental representations of on-field American football impact scenarios. Seven helmet-
 ed
 to-helmet impact configurations were simulated by propelling helmeted crash test dummies into each other. Head
 ite
 and helmet kinematics were measured with instrumentation and an optical motion capture system. The analysis of
 results, from 10 ms prior to the helmet contact to 20 ms after the loss of helmet contact, showed that the helmets
 translated 12 – 41 mm and rotated up to 37 degrees with respect to the head. The peak resultant linear
 d

 helmet ranged from 37% less to 71% more than the head, depending on the impact conditions. The results of this
 py
 study demonstrate that the kinematics of the head and helmet are noticeably different and that the helmet rotates
 significantly with respect to the head during impacts. Therefore, capturing the helmet kinematics using a video

 motion tracking methodology is not sufficient to study the biomechanics of the head. Head motion must be
 measured independently of the helmet.

 ABSTRACT
 Approximately 1.6-3.8 million sports-related traumatic brain injuries occur each year in the US. Researchers track
 the head motion using a variety of techniques to study the head injury biomechanics. To understand how helmets
 provide head protection, quantification of the relative motion between the head and the helmet is necessary. The
 purpose of this study was to compare helmet and head kinematics and quantify the relative motion of helmet with
 respect to head during experimental representations of on-field American football impact scenarios. Seven helmet-
 ed

 ite

 results, from 10 ms prior to the helmet contact to 20 ms after the loss of helmet contact, showed that the helmets
 translated 12 – 41 mm and rotated up to 37 degrees with respect to the head. The peak resultant linear

 helmet ranged from 37% less to 71% more than the head, depending on the impact conditions. The results of this
 py

 significantly with respect to the head during impacts. Therefore, capturing the helmet kinematics using a video
 Co
 motion tracking methodology is not sufficient to study the biomechanics of the head. Head motion must be
 measured independently of the helmet.

80	 and helmet kinematics and their relative motion contributes to elucidating the capabilities and
81	 limitations of head motion tracking methods, which are used to study the sports-related head
82	 injury mechanism.
83	 Second, data concerning the relative motion between the helmet and head may help
84	 improve helmet designs. Understanding the amount of translational and rotational motion
85	 allowed by current helmet systems is the first step to optimizing the use of that space. In
86	 addition, sufficiently detailed and accurate data characterizing motion of the helmet relative to
87	 the head will enable finite element models of the helmet and head to be validated, which will
88	 provide a useful virtual tool for improving helmet designs in the future. Computational
89	 simulation of experimental impact tests, for which the kinematics of the head and helmet are
90	 quantified, can be used to validate the head and helmet models and their interaction. The
91	 purpose of this study was to compare the kinematics of the helmet and head and quantify their
92	 relative motion during some generic on-field helmet-to-helmet football impacts with helmeted
93	 crash test dummies.
94	 MATERIALS AND METHODS
95	 Impact Reconstruction
96	 Two electric-powered belt-driven sled systems (McCarthy Engineering, Inc. Windsor,
97	 Ontario, Canada) were used to propel two helmeted 50th percentile male Hybrid III
98	 anthropomorphic test devices (ATDs) into each other to simulate seven generic helmet-to-
99	 helmet football impact configurations. The ATDs, with pedestrian pelvis modifications and no
100	 upper or lower extremities, were mounted to each sled using climbing harnesses and custom-
101	 made hinge joint release mechanisms bolted into the pedestrian pelvis femur attachment
102	 points. After accelerating to the desired speed, the sleds were rapidly decelerated, releasing
103	 the ATDs so that they were in free flight at the time of impact. Riddell Speed Classic (Riddell
104	 Inc., Chicago, IL) and Schutt Air XP Pro (Schutt Sports, Litchfield, IL) large-sized helmets were
105	 placed on the head of ATD 1 and ATD 2, respectively. Riddell and Schutt helmets are among the
106	 most commonly used helmets by football players [19, 20]. Large helmets were selected because
107	 large is the appropriate size to fit a Hybrid III 50th percentile male ATD head [16]. The friction
108	 between the Hybrid III head and helmet is significantly higher than that between a real human
109	 head and a football helmet [21]. A nylon skullcap was placed between the helmet and the head
110	 to facilitate helmet donning and reduce the friction [22-27]. Helmets were placed on the head
111	 using a NOCSAE positioning tool to position the brim of the helmet a consistent distance of 75
112	 mm from the nose of the headform.
113	 Seven impact configurations were created to represent generic concussive on-field
114	 helmet-to-helmet impacts. The generic test configurations were chosen to represent a variety
115	 of impact scenarios, including centered and eccentric impacts in front, side, and oblique d
116	 directions at closing speeds of 8 – 11 m/s (Figure 1). The closing speeds in this study were py
117	 chosen to represent concussive impacts based on a previous study in which it was determined
118	 that concussive helmet-to-helmet impacts in the NFL occurred at closing speeds of 9.3 ± 1.9
119	 m/s [16].
120	 The torso elevation was 60o for ATD 1 and 30o for ATD 2 in all tests. Configurations B and
121	 C were meant to be identical in terms of relative speeds of the ATDs with respect to each other
122	 but different in terms of absolute speeds of each ATD over the ground, as were configurations
123	 A and D. In practice, the launch trajectories varied slightly from run to run. Thus, the impact
124	 dynamics were not identical in these pairs of tests.
125	 [Figure 1] ed
126	 Measurement Systems
127	 The bulk motion of each helmet was measured using three redundant systems: one
128	 optical motion capture system and two sensor packages. All helmet measurements were taken
129	 at points on the helmet shell remote from the site of impact to avoid errors associated with
130	 focal deformation of the helmet shell near the point of impact. The coordinate system for the
131	 helmet was defined to be aligned with the head coordinate system prior to impact (x-anterior,
132	 y-right, z-down with the origin at the head center of gravity). Once the impact initiated, the
133	 location and orientation of the helmet coordinate frame were continuously updated with the
134	 helmet data as it diverged from the head coordinate system.
135	 The optical motion capture system (Vicon, Los Angeles, CA) tracked multiple
136	 retroreflective markers that were attached to the outer surface of each helmet with 18 cameras d
137	 at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz. All of the markers were used together to calculate an optimizedpy
138	 measurement of the position and rotational orientation of each helmet (Lessley et al., 2011).
139	 Based on a previous error analysis (Lessley et al., 2011), it was estimated that the motion
140	 capture data would measure helmet position with high accuracy (error < 1 mm). The motion
141	 capture data were filtered using a 50 Hz, low-pass, 4-pole Butterworth filter, then used to
142	 calculate the linear and angular velocity of each helmet over time. This cutoff frequency was
143	 chosen based on a Fast Fourier Transformation (FFT) analysis of the angular velocity data that
144	 showed that normalized amplitudes were less than 10% for frequencies greater than 50 Hz [28].
145	 In addition, each helmet was instrumented with two DTS 6DX-Pro sensors (Diversified
146	 Technical Systems, Seal Beach, CA) attached to the inner side of each helmet shell in locations
147	 that were not directly struck (Figure 2). The locations of sensors placed inside the helmets were
148	 different between the two helmets because the two helmets were struck in different places
149	 due to the difference between their initial elevation angle as well as their opposite facing
150	 directions (Figure 1). Each helmet sensor package had three accelerometers (2000 g range) and
151	 three angular rate sensors (18000 deg/s range). The helmet sensor packages had a mass of 12
152	 g (without cables) and dimensions of 19 × 19 × 14.5 mm. An additional sensor package
153	 consisting of six accelerometers (with similar characteristics as those of helmets) and three
154	 angular rate sensors (similar with those of helmets but with 8000-18000 deg/s rate, 6aω) was
155	 placed at the center of gravity of each Hybrid III dummy head. All sensor data, including the
156	 helmet and head instrumentation packages, were collected at 10 kHz using SLICE Micro and
157	 SLICE Nano in-dummy data acquisition systems (Diversified Technical Systems, Seal Beach, CA). ed
158	 For the head, the methodology described by Kang et al. [29] was used to calculate angular
159	 acceleration using the three additional coplanar, linear accelerometers. For the helmet sensor
160	 packages, the angular rate data was filtered, then differentiated using a central difference
161	 technique to calculate angular acceleration at each time step. The angular rate sensor data and
162	 the calculated angular accelerations were filtered by CFC 180. All other sensor data were
163	 filtered based on recommendations described in SAE J211 [30](Society of Automotive Engineers
164	 1995).
165	 [Figure 2]
166	 Having the initial position and orientation of helmet sensors as well as those of the
167	 helmet coordinate system, the data of helmet sensors were transferred to the helmet
168	 coordinate system using rigid body transformation equations [29]. Three-dimensional scans of
169	 the head and helmet, along with position data collected from a Romer Absolute Arm-6Axis
170	 (Exact Metrology, Cincinnati, OH) were used to establish the relationship between helmet
171	 landmarks, the helmet sensor packages, and the head coordinate system [29].
172	 The global reference frame was aligned with a fixed field reference frame used for the
173	 motion capture system (Figure 3). Motion capture marker locations on the helmet were used to
174	 establish 4×4 transformation matrices from the field coordinate system to the helmet
175	 coordinate systems (Figure 3). The transformation matrix between the head and helmet
176	 coordinate systems along with the motion capture (helmet-to-field) transformation matrices
177	 were used to establish the initial position of each dummy head center of gravity relative to the
178	 field coordinate system. These initial transformation matrices, sensor data, and methods ed
179	 described by Beard and Schlick [31] were used to update the helmet-to-field and head-to-field
180	 transformation matrices at each time point in order to calculate head and helmet kinematics in
181	 the field coordinate frame. Initial global positions and velocities were established using motion
182	 capture data 20 ms prior to impact, during the free-flight of each ATD. Accelerometer data
183	 were debiased by subtracting the average bias for each sensor over this time period, then
184	 adding back the components of gravitational acceleration. The sensor data were used to update
185	 the head-to-field and helmet-to-field transformation matrices at each time step, and the
186	 resulting array of transformation matrices was used to calculate head and helmet linear and
187	 angular accelerations, velocities, and positions.
188	 [Figure 3] nu
189	 Translational position data calculated from the sensor data were compared to the
190	 results from motion capture (as the gold standard). Drift in the accelerometer traces affected
191	 the double-integrated position data, which is a common issue [32]. To compensate for this drift,
192	 an optimization was performed to estimate the acceleration offset necessary to minimize the
193	 difference between the motion capture and helmet sensor-calculated global velocities for a
194	 desired post-impact time range. The end time range, during which minimal head-versus-helmet
195	 motion was present and impact vibrations had been damped, was established based on visual
196	 inspection of high speed videos. The error functions that were minimized to correct
197	 acceleration bias for the helmet and head sensors are provided below, where NRMSE is the
198	 normalized root mean square error over the desired post-impact time range, 𝑥, 𝑦, and 𝑧 are the
199	 axes, 𝑉 is the global velocity, and 𝑃 is the global position. The helmet sensor and head sensor
200	 indices refer to the kinematics measured by the sensors of helmet and head, respectively. ed
201	 Helmet motion capture system refers to the helmet kinematics obtained from reflection-based
202	 motion capture system. Because the velocity of head and helmet are assumed to be equal
203	 during the selected post-impact time ranges, minimizing the objective functions (1) and (2) (the
204	 difference between the head and helmet velocities) by tuning the acceleration offset as the
205	 decision variable results in finding the optimum acceleration offset value.

273	 RESULTS
274	 The peak resultant accelerations of the head and helmet were in the range of 29 – 121 g
275	 and 35 – 360 g, respectively. More specifically, the peak head resultant linear acceleration of
276	 ATD 1 and ATD 2 were 47 ± 14 g and 73 ± 22 g in tests A-D (front impacts), and 67 ± 2 g and 113
277	 ± 8 g in tests E-G (side and oblique impacts), respectively. The peak resultant linear acceleration
278	 of the helmet was 2 – 5 times higher than the head. The head and helmet of ATDs experienced
279	 a maximum resultant translational delta-v (defined as the post-impact velocity minus pre-
280	 impact velocity) of 3.9 – 8.5 m/s and 3.8 – 8.9 m/s, respectively. The measured peak resultant
281	 angular rates of the head and helmet were 13 - 375 rad/sec and 11 - 45 rad/sec, respectively, in
282	 different tests. In more detail, the peak head resultant angular velocity of ATD 1 and ATD 2
283	 were 22 ± 5 rad/sec and 20 ± 7 rad/sec in tests A-D, and 31 ± 1 rad/sec and 32 ± 4 rad/sec in
284	 tests E-G, respectively. Figure 5 shows an example of the time histories of resultant linear ed
285	 acceleration and angular velocity that the head and the helmet experienced during the tests
286	 (ATD1 in Test D). The peak resultant angular velocity of the helmet ranged from 37% less to
287	 71% more than the head, depending on the test configuration (Figure 6).
288	 An example of the time histories of relative displacement and rotation of the helmet
289	 with respect to the head is exhibited in Figure 7. During the impacts, the helmets translated 12
290	 – 41 mm (Figure 8) and rotated up to 37 degrees (Figure 9) with respect to the head. For the
291	 calculation of relative displacement and rotation, the position and orientation of the head were
292	 calculated using the head instrumentation, while the helmet kinematics were determined from
293	 multiple sources (i.e. helmet sensor data and optical motion capture system).
294	 [Figure 5], [Figure 6], [Figure 7 ],[Figure 8], [Figure 9]
295	 All the reported values are in the time range of 10 ms prior to the helmet contact to 20
296	 ms after the loss of helmet contact. The total time duration over which the computations were
297	 performed for each test was 60.8 ± 5.9 ms. Instrumentation Package No. 1 in the ATD 2 helmet
298	 failed during testing, so values are only available for one of the helmet sensor locations in that
299	 ATD. Additionally, the instrumentation package of ATD 2 failed to trigger in Test A, so the
300	 results are not available for ATD 2 in Test A.
301	 DISCUSSION
302	 The ATDs in this study experienced head impact severities ranging from relatively mild
303	 to moderately severe compared to previous dummy reconstructions of concussive impacts in
304	 the NFL [17]. The peak resultant acceleration measured by the helmet accelerometers at the
305	 helmet local coordinate system origin was 2-5 times higher than that of the head. The present d
306	 study shows that even with the accelerometers far from the impact location, the peak py
307	 acceleration of the helmet shell is much higher than the head. Co
308	 The large differences between peak helmet and head accelerations are the result of
309	 vibration and inertial effects. Since the viscoelastic padding inside the helmet stores a portion
310	 of energy and dissipates the rest, the shell acceleration, especially the vibrational part, does not
311	 fully transfer to the head. Moreover, in some cases the helmet acceleration peak occurs at the
312	 beginning of the impact when the head and helmet are not initially coupled. The impact force is
313	 initially applied only to the lightweight helmet shell, which results in higher accelerations in
314	 accordance with Newton’s second law (force equals mass times acceleration).
315	 In most cases of this study, the helmet was forcibly translated, which caused the
316	 dummy’s head to rotate due to the constraints of the neck. In these cases, the rotation of the
317	 dummy’s head was resisted by the helmet (rather than caused by it), and the peak angular
318	 velocity of the head was higher than the helmet. ATD 1 experienced this type of impact in Test
319	 C, when the impact to the front of the helmet caused the head to rotate rearward faster than
320	 the helmet. In a few cases, the helmet was forcibly rotated, and the rotation of the helmet
321	 forced the head to rotate due to fit constraints and friction between the helmet and head. In
322	 these cases, the peak angular velocity of the helmet was higher than the head. ATD 1
323	 experienced this type of impact in test B, when the crown of ATD 2’s helmet snagged the brow
324	 of ATD 1’s facemask and pulled the front of the helmet down over the eyes of the ATD 1. This
325	 observation presents a challenge to helmet designers because the angular velocity of the head ed
326	 is best reduced by tightly coupling the head and helmet in some impacts while decoupling the
327	 head and helmet in other impacts.
328	 The resultant linear acceleration and angular velocity of heads and helmets tended to be
329	 higher in Tests E, F, and G than the other tests (Appendix Tables A1 and A4) due to two main
330	 reasons. First, the closing velocities in those tests were greater than the other tests. Second,
331	 because the impact directions of those tests were not in a plane parallel to the dummy’s
332	 sagittal plane, the impact forces were applied to a lower effective mass compared to the other
333	 tests
334	 Displacement of helmet shell with respect to the head is caused by compression and
335	 shearing of the padding (as well as slip between the padding and the head if it occurs). In this
336	 study, the displacement of the helmet relative to the head ranged from 12 to 41 mm, which
337	 appeared reasonable considering the thickness of the padding. The distance between the bare
338	 dummy head and the outer surface of the shell was 47 - 57 mm for the Riddell Speed Classic
339	 and 39 - 64 mm for Schutt Air XP, depending on the location [34]. In most cases, the movement
340	 of the helmet relative to the head was primarily downward (+z direction). There were several
341	 reasons for this. First, most impacts involved the top portion of the helmet. Second, the dummy
342	 neck is very stiff axially, which means that downward motion of the helmet results primarily in
343	 padding compression whereas fore-aft or lateral helmet motion results primarily in head
344	 acceleration. Third, the helmet padding was thicker on the top than the sides or back.
345	 The rotation of the helmet with respect to the head during an impact can be substantial
346	 (Figure 9). For example, in Test B and Test E, the helmet of ATD 1 experienced a sagittal y-
347	 rotation of about -35 degrees with respect to the head (the brow of the helmet was pulled
348	 down over the eyes of the dummy). The coronal x-rotation was slightly greater for d
349	 configurations E - G compared to other configurations (except for the ATD 1 in Test F) becausepy
350	 the ATDs hit each other laterally. Co
351	 The redundant measurements of relative displacement between the helmet and head
352	 taken by the helmet sensors and the motion capture system were in good agreement (Figures 6
353	 – 9). The finding that the two helmet sensor packages in ATD 1 gave consistent results for all
354	 the tests validated our assumption that the helmet shell behaves as a rigid body at points
355	 remote from the site of impact. Differences in relative displacement (Figure 8) calculated using
356	 the helmet sensors versus the optical motion capture system may be attributed to a
357	 combination of sensor drift (arising from double-integration of accelerometer data), local
358	 helmet deformation, and localized helmet vibration. To quantify the drift error, acceleration
359	 data was filtered, debiased, and double-integrated for each test during the time for which the
360	 ATDs were stationary. Knowing that there was no actual displacement, the calculated
361	 displacement from this exercise could be used to approximate the error accumulated over the
362	 impact duration for an individual sensor package. This exercise resulted in an estimation of less
363	 than 1 mm of error accumulated over 80 ms. Even with a debiasing error of 0.1 g (which was
364	 estimated to be the maximum possible error), the accumulated displacement error over 80 ms
365	 would be 3 mm. On the other hand, because the motion capture system used multiple
366	 reflective markers at different locations on the helmet to track its position, it was affected by
367	 the localized helmet deformations and vibrations less than the sensors. A combination of these
368	 factors resulted in the difference between the calculated relative displacements of the helmet
369	 with respect to the head by motion capture and sensor data. ed
370	 Two commonly used helmet by football players were utilized in this study and the d
371	 results cannot be generalized to all type of helmets. While some helmet designers seek a tightpy
372	 coupling between head and helmet, others allow the head to further rotate inside the helmet.
373	 Hence, it is expected to see different results if testing with another helmet for which the design
374	 idea is different.
375	 A limitation of this study is that relative motion of the head and helmet was estimated
376	 using the Hybrid III, which lacks biofidelity in certain impact scenarios [35, 36]. In addition, each
377	 test scenario was performed only once. Further, the relative motion of the helmet with respect
378	 to the head might vary with differences in the tightness of helmet fit and chin strap tightness,
379	 as well as be affected by a player’s hair and perspiration [16]. To mitigate some of the
380	 differences between the Hybrid III and human head, a large-sized helmet was used which has
381	 been shown to represent the proper fit of a football helmet on a Hybrid III headform [16]. The
382	 friction coefficient between the Hybrid III head and a football helmet is bigger than a human’s
383	 head [21]. To reduce the friction between the helmet and head, we placed a nylon stocking
384	 over the dummy’s head. This approach has been used in several previous studies [21-26], and
385	 although it cannot represent the whole spectrum of friction characteristics in players having
386	 varied hairstyles, it is at least representative of those players who wear a nylon skullcap. The
387	 magnitude of friction between the head and helmet are expected to play a significant role in
388	 their interaction and can especially affect the rotation of helmet with respect to the head.
389	 Further studies are required to quantify this effect.
390	 The results of this study demonstrate the limitations of helmet-mounted sensors
391	 intended to characterize the head impact exposure, such as the HITS [15, 23-25] or the gForce
392	 Tracker [41]. In the HIT system, springs or foam press the sensors onto the head in order to d
393	 improve coupling between the sensors and the head when measuring translational py
394	 acceleration. However, no current helmet-based sensor employs a method to ensure rotational
395	 coupling between the sensors and the head. The results of this study indicate that
396	 measurements of angular velocity from helmet-based sensors could be in error by as much as
397	 71% (Figure 6). Some researchers try to characterize the head impacts [37, 38] or develop a
398	 threshold for brain injury using head kinematics and clinical reports [39] in football. Using the
399	 kinematics of the helmet instead of the head might result in making wrong conclusions. For
400	 example, considering the fact that the peak acceleration of helmet was found to be greater
401	 than the head in the present study as well as some studies in the past [18, 40], it is expected
402	 that an effort to find an injury threshold for the peak acceleration of head using the kinematics
403	 of helmet result in overestimating the threshold. Although using methods that estimate the
404	 head kinematics from the helmet kinematics [40] might mitigate such effects, the estimated
405	 values have potential to error due to uncertainties in impact condition such as helmet fit,
406	 impact velocity, direction and location, and the combinations of those factors.
407	 Despite the limitations, this study enriches our understanding of the relative motion of
408	 the helmet with respect to the head during football impacts. The results of this investigation
409	 are useful for evaluating the capabilities and limitations of the available methods and
410	 techniques for tracking head motion during impacts in helmeted sports. This research
411	 reinforces the idea that successful quantification of head kinematics requires measurement of
412	 the head acceleration independent from the helmet [41-43]. In addition, capturing both the
413	 head and helmet kinematics is necessary to study the biomechanics of impact when using a ed
414	 video motion tracking methodology.
415	 CONCLUSION py
416	 Seven generic on-field helmet-to-helmet football impact scenarios were simulated Co
417	 experimentally with helmeted crash test dummies and the kinematics of head and helmet were
418	 measured during the impacts. In our tests, the peak linear acceleration of the helmet was 2 – 5
419	 times greater than the head and the helmet translated 12 – 41 mm relative to the head,
420	 primarily downward. The peak angular velocity of helmet was greater than the head in some
421	 tests and less in others. In some tests, the helmet rotated more than 30° relative to the head.
422	 This study quantifies the helmet motion with respect to the head in potentially concussive
423	 impacts, which is important for understanding the mechanisms by which helmets can mitigate
424	 the transfer of force and momentum to the head.
425	 ACKNOWLEDGMENT ce
426	 The views expressed are solely those of the authors and do not represent those of
427	 Football Research, Inc. (FRI) or any of its affiliates or funding sources. The authors would like to
428	 acknowledge McCarthy Engineering Inc., Biocore LLC, and the University of Virginia Center for
429	 Applied Biomechanics for their technical and equipment support.
430	 FUNDING
431	 The research presented in this paper was made possible by a grant from FRI.

 Second, data concerning the relative motion between the helmet and head may help
 improve helmet designs. Understanding the amount of translational and rotational motion
 allowed by current helmet systems is the first step to optimizing the use of that space. In
 addition, sufficiently detailed and accurate data characterizing motion of the helmet relative to
 the head will enable finite element models of the helmet and head to be validated, which will
 provide a useful virtual tool for improving helmet designs in the future. Computational
 simulation of experimental impact tests, for which the kinematics of the head and helmet are
 quantified, can be used to validate the head and helmet models and their interaction. The
 purpose of this study was to compare the kinematics of the helmet and head and quantify their
 relative motion during some generic on-field helmet-to-helmet football impacts with helmeted
 crash test dummies.
 MATERIALS AND METHODS
 Impact Reconstruction
 Two electric-powered belt-driven sled systems (McCarthy Engineering, Inc. Windsor,
 Ontario, Canada) were used to propel two helmeted 50th percentile male Hybrid III
 anthropomorphic test devices (ATDs) into each other to simulate seven generic helmet-to-
 helmet football impact configurations. The ATDs, with pedestrian pelvis modifications and no
 upper or lower extremities, were mounted to each sled using climbing harnesses and custom-
 made hinge joint release mechanisms bolted into the pedestrian pelvis femur attachment
 points. After accelerating to the desired speed, the sleds were rapidly decelerated, releasing
 the ATDs so that they were in free flight at the time of impact. Riddell Speed Classic (Riddell
 Inc., Chicago, IL) and Schutt Air XP Pro (Schutt Sports, Litchfield, IL) large-sized helmets were
 placed on the head of ATD 1 and ATD 2, respectively. Riddell and Schutt helmets are among the
 most commonly used helmets by football players [19, 20]. Large helmets were selected because
 large is the appropriate size to fit a Hybrid III 50th percentile male ATD head [16]. The friction
 between the Hybrid III head and helmet is significantly higher than that between a real human
 head and a football helmet [21]. A nylon skullcap was placed between the helmet and the head
 to facilitate helmet donning and reduce the friction [22-27]. Helmets were placed on the head
 using a NOCSAE positioning tool to position the brim of the helmet a consistent distance of 75
 mm from the nose of the headform.
 Seven impact configurations were created to represent generic concussive on-field
 helmet-to-helmet impacts. The generic test configurations were chosen to represent a variety
 of impact scenarios, including centered and eccentric impacts in front, side, and oblique d
 directions at closing speeds of 8 – 11 m/s (Figure 1). The closing speeds in this study were py
 chosen to represent concussive impacts based on a previous study in which it was determined
 that concussive helmet-to-helmet impacts in the NFL occurred at closing speeds of 9.3 ± 1.9
 m/s [16].
 The torso elevation was 60o for ATD 1 and 30o for ATD 2 in all tests. Configurations B and
 C were meant to be identical in terms of relative speeds of the ATDs with respect to each other
 but different in terms of absolute speeds of each ATD over the ground, as were configurations
 A and D. In practice, the launch trajectories varied slightly from run to run. Thus, the impact
 dynamics were not identical in these pairs of tests.
 [Figure 1] ed
 Measurement Systems
 The bulk motion of each helmet was measured using three redundant systems: one
 optical motion capture system and two sensor packages. All helmet measurements were taken
 at points on the helmet shell remote from the site of impact to avoid errors associated with
 focal deformation of the helmet shell near the point of impact. The coordinate system for the
 helmet was defined to be aligned with the head coordinate system prior to impact (x-anterior,
 y-right, z-down with the origin at the head center of gravity). Once the impact initiated, the
 location and orientation of the helmet coordinate frame were continuously updated with the
 helmet data as it diverged from the head coordinate system.
 The optical motion capture system (Vicon, Los Angeles, CA) tracked multiple
 retroreflective markers that were attached to the outer surface of each helmet with 18 cameras d
 at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz. All of the markers were used together to calculate an optimizedpy
 measurement of the position and rotational orientation of each helmet (Lessley et al., 2011).
 Based on a previous error analysis (Lessley et al., 2011), it was estimated that the motion
 capture data would measure helmet position with high accuracy (error < 1 mm). The motion
 capture data were filtered using a 50 Hz, low-pass, 4-pole Butterworth filter, then used to
 calculate the linear and angular velocity of each helmet over time. This cutoff frequency was
 chosen based on a Fast Fourier Transformation (FFT) analysis of the angular velocity data that
 showed that normalized amplitudes were less than 10% for frequencies greater than 50 Hz [28].
 In addition, each helmet was instrumented with two DTS 6DX-Pro sensors (Diversified
 Technical Systems, Seal Beach, CA) attached to the inner side of each helmet shell in locations
 that were not directly struck (Figure 2). The locations of sensors placed inside the helmets were
 different between the two helmets because the two helmets were struck in different places
 due to the difference between their initial elevation angle as well as their opposite facing
 directions (Figure 1). Each helmet sensor package had three accelerometers (2000 g range) and
 three angular rate sensors (18000 deg/s range). The helmet sensor packages had a mass of 12
 g (without cables) and dimensions of 19 × 19 × 14.5 mm. An additional sensor package
 consisting of six accelerometers (with similar characteristics as those of helmets) and three
 angular rate sensors (similar with those of helmets but with 8000-18000 deg/s rate, 6aω) was
 placed at the center of gravity of each Hybrid III dummy head. All sensor data, including the
 helmet and head instrumentation packages, were collected at 10 kHz using SLICE Micro and
 SLICE Nano in-dummy data acquisition systems (Diversified Technical Systems, Seal Beach, CA). ed
 For the head, the methodology described by Kang et al. [29] was used to calculate angular
 acceleration using the three additional coplanar, linear accelerometers. For the helmet sensor
 packages, the angular rate data was filtered, then differentiated using a central difference
 technique to calculate angular acceleration at each time step. The angular rate sensor data and
 the calculated angular accelerations were filtered by CFC 180. All other sensor data were
 filtered based on recommendations described in SAE J211 [30](Society of Automotive Engineers
 1995).
 [Figure 2]
 Having the initial position and orientation of helmet sensors as well as those of the
 helmet coordinate system, the data of helmet sensors were transferred to the helmet
 coordinate system using rigid body transformation equations [29]. Three-dimensional scans of
 the head and helmet, along with position data collected from a Romer Absolute Arm-6Axis
 (Exact Metrology, Cincinnati, OH) were used to establish the relationship between helmet
 landmarks, the helmet sensor packages, and the head coordinate system [29].
 The global reference frame was aligned with a fixed field reference frame used for the
 motion capture system (Figure 3). Motion capture marker locations on the helmet were used to
 establish 4×4 transformation matrices from the field coordinate system to the helmet
 coordinate systems (Figure 3). The transformation matrix between the head and helmet
 coordinate systems along with the motion capture (helmet-to-field) transformation matrices
 were used to establish the initial position of each dummy head center of gravity relative to the
 field coordinate system. These initial transformation matrices, sensor data, and methods ed
 described by Beard and Schlick [31] were used to update the helmet-to-field and head-to-field
 transformation matrices at each time point in order to calculate head and helmet kinematics in
 the field coordinate frame. Initial global positions and velocities were established using motion
 capture data 20 ms prior to impact, during the free-flight of each ATD. Accelerometer data
 were debiased by subtracting the average bias for each sensor over this time period, then
 adding back the components of gravitational acceleration. The sensor data were used to update
 the head-to-field and helmet-to-field transformation matrices at each time step, and the
 resulting array of transformation matrices was used to calculate head and helmet linear and
 angular accelerations, velocities, and positions.

 The peak resultant accelerations of the head and helmet were in the range of 29 – 121 g
 and 35 – 360 g, respectively. More specifically, the peak head resultant linear acceleration of
 ATD 1 and ATD 2 were 47 ± 14 g and 73 ± 22 g in tests A-D (front impacts), and 67 ± 2 g and 113
 ± 8 g in tests E-G (side and oblique impacts), respectively. The peak resultant linear acceleration
 of the helmet was 2 – 5 times higher than the head. The head and helmet of ATDs experienced
 a maximum resultant translational delta-v (defined as the post-impact velocity minus pre-
 impact velocity) of 3.9 – 8.5 m/s and 3.8 – 8.9 m/s, respectively. The measured peak resultant
 angular rates of the head and helmet were 13 - 375 rad/sec and 11 - 45 rad/sec, respectively, in
 different tests. In more detail, the peak head resultant angular velocity of ATD 1 and ATD 2
 were 22 ± 5 rad/sec and 20 ± 7 rad/sec in tests A-D, and 31 ± 1 rad/sec and 32 ± 4 rad/sec in
 tests E-G, respectively. Figure 5 shows an example of the time histories of resultant linear ed
 acceleration and angular velocity that the head and the helmet experienced during the tests
 (ATD1 in Test D). The peak resultant angular velocity of the helmet ranged from 37% less to
 71% more than the head, depending on the test configuration (Figure 6).
 An example of the time histories of relative displacement and rotation of the helmet
 with respect to the head is exhibited in Figure 7. During the impacts, the helmets translated 12
 – 41 mm (Figure 8) and rotated up to 37 degrees (Figure 9) with respect to the head. For the
 calculation of relative displacement and rotation, the position and orientation of the head were
 calculated using the head instrumentation, while the helmet kinematics were determined from
 multiple sources (i.e. helmet sensor data and optical motion capture system).
 [Figure 5], [Figure 6], [Figure 7 ],[Figure 8], [Figure 9]
 All the reported values are in the time range of 10 ms prior to the helmet contact to 20
 ms after the loss of helmet contact. The total time duration over which the computations were
 performed for each test was 60.8 ± 5.9 ms. Instrumentation Package No. 1 in the ATD 2 helmet
 failed during testing, so values are only available for one of the helmet sensor locations in that
 ATD. Additionally, the instrumentation package of ATD 2 failed to trigger in Test A, so the
 results are not available for ATD 2 in Test A.
 DISCUSSION
 The ATDs in this study experienced head impact severities ranging from relatively mild
 to moderately severe compared to previous dummy reconstructions of concussive impacts in
 the NFL [17]. The peak resultant acceleration measured by the helmet accelerometers at the
 helmet local coordinate system origin was 2-5 times higher than that of the head. The present d
 study shows that even with the accelerometers far from the impact location, the peak py
 acceleration of the helmet shell is much higher than the head. Co
 The large differences between peak helmet and head accelerations are the result of
 vibration and inertial effects. Since the viscoelastic padding inside the helmet stores a portion
 of energy and dissipates the rest, the shell acceleration, especially the vibrational part, does not
 fully transfer to the head. Moreover, in some cases the helmet acceleration peak occurs at the
 beginning of the impact when the head and helmet are not initially coupled. The impact force is
 initially applied only to the lightweight helmet shell, which results in higher accelerations in
 accordance with Newton’s second law (force equals mass times acceleration).
 In most cases of this study, the helmet was forcibly translated, which caused the
 dummy’s head to rotate due to the constraints of the neck. In these cases, the rotation of the
 dummy’s head was resisted by the helmet (rather than caused by it), and the peak angular
 velocity of the head was higher than the helmet. ATD 1 experienced this type of impact in Test
 C, when the impact to the front of the helmet caused the head to rotate rearward faster than
 the helmet. In a few cases, the helmet was forcibly rotated, and the rotation of the helmet
 forced the head to rotate due to fit constraints and friction between the helmet and head. In
 these cases, the peak angular velocity of the helmet was higher than the head. ATD 1
 experienced this type of impact in test B, when the crown of ATD 2’s helmet snagged the brow
 of ATD 1’s facemask and pulled the front of the helmet down over the eyes of the ATD 1. This
 observation presents a challenge to helmet designers because the angular velocity of the head ed
 is best reduced by tightly coupling the head and helmet in some impacts while decoupling the
 head and helmet in other impacts.
 The resultant linear acceleration and angular velocity of heads and helmets tended to be
 higher in Tests E, F, and G than the other tests (Appendix Tables A1 and A4) due to two main
 reasons. First, the closing velocities in those tests were greater than the other tests. Second,
 because the impact directions of those tests were not in a plane parallel to the dummy’s
 sagittal plane, the impact forces were applied to a lower effective mass compared to the other
 tests
 Displacement of helmet shell with respect to the head is caused by compression and
 shearing of the padding (as well as slip between the padding and the head if it occurs). In this
 study, the displacement of the helmet relative to the head ranged from 12 to 41 mm, which
 appeared reasonable considering the thickness of the padding. The distance between the bare
 dummy head and the outer surface of the shell was 47 - 57 mm for the Riddell Speed Classic
 and 39 - 64 mm for Schutt Air XP, depending on the location [34]. In most cases, the movement
 of the helmet relative to the head was primarily downward (+z direction). There were several
 reasons for this. First, most impacts involved the top portion of the helmet. Second, the dummy
 neck is very stiff axially, which means that downward motion of the helmet results primarily in
 padding compression whereas fore-aft or lateral helmet motion results primarily in head
 acceleration. Third, the helmet padding was thicker on the top than the sides or back.
 The rotation of the helmet with respect to the head during an impact can be substantial
 (Figure 9). For example, in Test B and Test E, the helmet of ATD 1 experienced a sagittal y-
 rotation of about -35 degrees with respect to the head (the brow of the helmet was pulled
 down over the eyes of the dummy). The coronal x-rotation was slightly greater for d
 configurations E - G compared to other configurations (except for the ATD 1 in Test F) becausepy
 the ATDs hit each other laterally. Co
 The redundant measurements of relative displacement between the helmet and head
 taken by the helmet sensors and the motion capture system were in good agreement (Figures 6
 – 9). The finding that the two helmet sensor packages in ATD 1 gave consistent results for all
 the tests validated our assumption that the helmet shell behaves as a rigid body at points
 remote from the site of impact. Differences in relative displacement (Figure 8) calculated using
 the helmet sensors versus the optical motion capture system may be attributed to a
 combination of sensor drift (arising from double-integration of accelerometer data), local
 helmet deformation, and localized helmet vibration. To quantify the drift error, acceleration
 data was filtered, debiased, and double-integrated for each test during the time for which the
 ATDs were stationary. Knowing that there was no actual displacement, the calculated
 displacement from this exercise could be used to approximate the error accumulated over the
 impact duration for an individual sensor package. This exercise resulted in an estimation of less
 than 1 mm of error accumulated over 80 ms. Even with a debiasing error of 0.1 g (which was
 estimated to be the maximum possible error), the accumulated displacement error over 80 ms
 would be 3 mm. On the other hand, because the motion capture system used multiple
 reflective markers at different locations on the helmet to track its position, it was affected by
 the localized helmet deformations and vibrations less than the sensors. A combination of these
 factors resulted in the difference between the calculated relative displacements of the helmet
 with respect to the head by motion capture and sensor data. ed
 Two commonly used helmet by football players were utilized in this study and the d
 results cannot be generalized to all type of helmets. While some helmet designers seek a tightpy
 coupling between head and helmet, others allow the head to further rotate inside the helmet.
 Hence, it is expected to see different results if testing with another helmet for which the design
 idea is different.
 A limitation of this study is that relative motion of the head and helmet was estimated
 using the Hybrid III, which lacks biofidelity in certain impact scenarios [35, 36]. In addition, each
 test scenario was performed only once. Further, the relative motion of the helmet with respect
 to the head might vary with differences in the tightness of helmet fit and chin strap tightness,
 as well as be affected by a player’s hair and perspiration [16]. To mitigate some of the
 differences between the Hybrid III and human head, a large-sized helmet was used which has
 been shown to represent the proper fit of a football helmet on a Hybrid III headform [16]. The
 friction coefficient between the Hybrid III head and a football helmet is bigger than a human’s
 head [21]. To reduce the friction between the helmet and head, we placed a nylon stocking
 over the dummy’s head. This approach has been used in several previous studies [21-26], and
 although it cannot represent the whole spectrum of friction characteristics in players having
 varied hairstyles, it is at least representative of those players who wear a nylon skullcap. The
 magnitude of friction between the head and helmet are expected to play a significant role in
 their interaction and can especially affect the rotation of helmet with respect to the head.
 Further studies are required to quantify this effect.
 The results of this study demonstrate the limitations of helmet-mounted sensors
 intended to characterize the head impact exposure, such as the HITS [15, 23-25] or the gForce
 Tracker [41]. In the HIT system, springs or foam press the sensors onto the head in order to d
 improve coupling between the sensors and the head when measuring translational py
 acceleration. However, no current helmet-based sensor employs a method to ensure rotational
 coupling between the sensors and the head. The results of this study indicate that
 measurements of angular velocity from helmet-based sensors could be in error by as much as
 71% (Figure 6). Some researchers try to characterize the head impacts [37, 38] or develop a
 threshold for brain injury using head kinematics and clinical reports [39] in football. Using the
 kinematics of the helmet instead of the head might result in making wrong conclusions. For
 example, considering the fact that the peak acceleration of helmet was found to be greater
 than the head in the present study as well as some studies in the past [18, 40], it is expected
 that an effort to find an injury threshold for the peak acceleration of head using the kinematics
 of helmet result in overestimating the threshold. Although using methods that estimate the
 head kinematics from the helmet kinematics [40] might mitigate such effects, the estimated
 values have potential to error due to uncertainties in impact condition such as helmet fit,
 impact velocity, direction and location, and the combinations of those factors.
 Despite the limitations, this study enriches our understanding of the relative motion of
 the helmet with respect to the head during football impacts. The results of this investigation
 are useful for evaluating the capabilities and limitations of the available methods and
 techniques for tracking head motion during impacts in helmeted sports. This research
 reinforces the idea that successful quantification of head kinematics requires measurement of
 the head acceleration independent from the helmet [41-43]. In addition, capturing both the
 head and helmet kinematics is necessary to study the biomechanics of impact when using a ed
 video motion tracking methodology.
 CONCLUSION py
 Seven generic on-field helmet-to-helmet football impact scenarios were simulated Co
 experimentally with helmeted crash test dummies and the kinematics of head and helmet were
 measured during the impacts. In our tests, the peak linear acceleration of the helmet was 2 – 5
 times greater than the head and the helmet translated 12 – 41 mm relative to the head,
 primarily downward. The peak angular velocity of helmet was greater than the head in some
 tests and less in others. In some tests, the helmet rotated more than 30° relative to the head.
 This study quantifies the helmet motion with respect to the head in potentially concussive
 impacts, which is important for understanding the mechanisms by which helmets can mitigate
 the transfer of force and momentum to the head.
 ACKNOWLEDGMENT ce
 The views expressed are solely those of the authors and do not represent those of
 Football Research, Inc. (FRI) or any of its affiliates or funding sources. The authors would like to
 acknowledge McCarthy Engineering Inc., Biocore LLC, and the University of Virginia Center for
 Applied Biomechanics for their technical and equipment support.

 The research presented in this paper was made possible by a grant from FRI.
